This is a horrible basket, lol.

A way better one (just tokens) would be:

1. $HYPE for exposure to decentralized exchange space increasing volumes 10x as agents enable. Agents helping you invest may prefer to use Hype as its the most liquid venue + has the most credibility right now. The reason why you go max size into Hype here is that liquduity begets more liquidity and Hype has the most — agents will really like that.

2. $LIT on the same above thesis but under the pretense that agents calculate that the average trade size for people trading with agents would benefit from no taker fees like Lit’s model. Only caveat here would be that Lit will have serious investor unlock overhang. 

3. $ZRO as a bet that agents will be seamlessly moving collateral across chains AND that ATLAS actually scales to the point where the performance gains start to lead to better liquduity. Their fee profile is also advantageous for retail types of traders as well. This reality is more of a moonshot but unlocks end in a couple months and institutional partnerships leading to official asset issuance, like DTCC and tokenized equities, could lead to agents preferring their rails. 

4. $ZEC as agentic AI increases activity, ZCash will ensure anonymity + may be a preferred currency for agents to recommend storing valuing in in comparison to BTC.

5. $NEAR as a combination of exposure to interop with NEAR intents, AI, and privacy.

6. $BP as exposure to tokenized assets on Solana which is highly liquid already + has a lot of existing float of stables / liqduity for people to move into spot assets onchain without having to be educated.

7. $PUMP as agents reduce friction to buying and Pump is the best onchain casino, their flows are already exploding w Fomo, agents bringing in new class of users will lead to more participants in the casino.

7. $SOL would likely reprice if BP AND Pump both do well (rotate memecoin profits into major stocks / SOL is a good expansion of last cycles store value in SOL).

8. $PRL as a make it bag — Proof of Useful Work enables miners to do matmul (math used for training and inference) which can be backed by the token issued after that work is used in an actual exchange of dollars for AI token to the miner that provided the GPU. This is what most of the smart people are excited about (same crowd talking about it that were talking about ZEC pre re-rating). Only caveat is that it’s very hard to acquire right now and there are some concerns of Chinese miners cornering a majority of float.

9. $VVV for private inference + utility token derived strictly from AI inference increasing. Has already moved a ton and there are some concerns that the token model is unsustainable but gives you direct exposure to the thesis.

The one thing to remember about AI is that it does very well when there is a verifiable reward to optimize for. If most users intents going to Muse / Instinct are some form of economic action posed as a question, the agent will seek to perform the task by quantifying the question and then searching for what its training data considers “right.”

No one is going to ask the agent “which oracle is the best and most decentralized” in which it would likely answer “$LINK”. 

They’re going to ask “How do I buy Bitcoin with leverage?” And it’s going to search its weights, read Twitter, check the order books, and conclude “Hyperliquid.”

See what I mean?

That’s why picking the major category winners for what agents will likely care about (trading, privacy, asset issuance, gambling, and inference) will outperform this cycle as we are fully in the app-specific token era.

text:
i lacked the spells and incantations

these past couple of days, i’ve been trying to do a little more cad design, making things i eventually want to 3d print.

i didn’t lack the ambition. i didn’t lack the desire to make something and will it into existence. i just didn’t have the spells and incantations i needed to make it at the level i wanted to.

i lacked the vocabulary.

and for the first time in a while, i really had to learn.

i had to learn about what makes 3d printing possible, how to make parts more efficient and durable, and how to think about the real world. i had to develop the words to describe curvature and shape, and what i wanted those things to feel like.

it’s made me appreciate things so much more. i’m starting to understand why the curves on apple devices are so beautiful, and how much work has gone into them. i appreciate the physical space around me more, and what it takes to build the things in it.

i keep coming back to this idea that ai really is magic. we’re all magicians and mages now, but we still have to learn the spells and incantations.

the more i work with it, the less i believe that the advent of ai will cause us to stop learning. for me, it’s been the opposite. having the ability to make something has made me want to understand it more deeply.

language isn’t unique to humanity, of course. but i think our ability to find the words for what we want is going to carry us further now.

if you have the courage and the ambition to want something, you can start learning the spells and the incantation to bring it into the world.

text:
Doomerism approach is never a helpful framing, even if it starts with "calmly" and with best intentions. 

What we need is risk assessment, practical timelines, and actionable plan.

AI is starting to overturn some of the long-held assumptions on mathematical complexity. At the same time risk of more intelligence applied to these problems yielding new surprising results is growing. But so far, we haven't seen practical security timelines for elliptic cruves materially changing.  It's important for crypto space to keep vigilance and flexibility, but speculating about specific "months" timeline creates an unnecessary panic.

Going "bunker mode" is not practical nor a safe approach given how complex it is in operations. We can have better approaches here, for example by recording recovery PQC keys in parallel on application level.

Better approach is making sure that blockchains and tooling around them is designed with cryptographic agility in mind, allowing to evolve cryptography and let users easily update without sacrificing user experience.

NEAR account model was design with this in mind from the start - ability to manage and rotate keys, add and remove supported cryptography. 

NEAR already supports post-quantum ML-DSA and we are planning to add hash-based cryptography too over time. 

User can just rotate keys on your accounts without needing to move anything or have a complex operations.

Industry should accelerate post-quantum readiness, not because we have updated timelines, but because upgrading cryptography should be a routine operation, not a crisis response.
author: tarunchitra
quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

quoted_text:
A lot of people interpreted this post in many different ways. I did not realize it would be viewed almost 4M times and that it would end up being one of my most liked posts on this platform, so I wanted to expand on it a bit. If you watched any of my recent videos, all of what I'm about to say are things you have already heard.

I think admitting when we are wrong about something is important, as it helps us grow as investors and hopefully allows us to make fewer mistakes in the future.

It also communicates to those who choose to listen to our views that we recognize we are fallible. Pretending to be right about everything is silly, and gaslighting an audience by saying "exactly as predicted" about everything is exhausting and not representative of the truth.

I also really appreciate all the support many of you showed. It genuinely means a lot. My goal in being on here has always been to help people navigate markets, so when I get something wrong, I think it is important to acknowledge it rather than pretend it did not happen.

Since many people took the original post to mean different things, I wanted to clarify what I was actually admitting I was wrong about.

Specifically, my post was about Bitcoin taking out the May high, which I had repeatedly said I did not think would happen.

If I spend two months saying something is unlikely to happen, and then it happens, I cannot sit here and pretend like I was calling for it when I wasn't.

Because of that, I felt I needed to acknowledge that I was wrong. I wish I had not been as deterministic, and that I had been more open-minded to the possibility of a higher high. I should hold myself accountable for my views by admitting when I get things wrong.

But that is all my post was meant to convey.

Some of the narratives that have developed from that post are not fully representative of my views.

Bitcoin is still operating under a difficult macro backdrop that has caused it to underperform other markets for years. Until liquidity conditions improve, I think that relative underperformance could remain an issue. That does not mean Bitcoin cannot have rallies or bull markets, but it could mean that the gains are not as significant as they were during periods when liquidity was more free-flowing.

Being wrong about the May high also does not automatically mean that I relinquish every other view I have expressed.

I have discussed the possibility of Q4 2026 weakness since Q4 2025. With one week left before Q4 begins, I do not think Bitcoin making a higher high means I should suddenly pretend that view never existed. What it does mean is that I should be less deterministic about it and more willing to change my view as new information comes in.

As long as Bitcoin remains above the May high, I have to respect the breakout. Continued acceptance above the range highs would increasingly challenge my broader bear market thesis, which I have honestly had a hard time letting go of. 

If Bitcoin instead closes a weekly candle back below the May high, then I think weakness into Q4 remains possible. Even then, the fact that Bitcoin already made a higher high could change what that weakness ultimately looks like. Q4 weakness would not necessarily require a new low.

And importantly, if Bitcoin does show weakness in Q4, it does not change the fact that I was wrong about what Bitcoin already accomplished in Q3. I would rather use that experience to hopefully become a better investor than pretend it did not happen.

The part I am still struggling to reconcile is the macro backdrop.

Long-end yields have continued to rise, alongside the dollar and energy. I would normally expect that combination to eventually pressure long-duration assets like crypto.

I do not fully understand Bitcoin's move to $87K from a macro perspective, but I can understand it from a technical analysis perspective (golden cross, RSI, etc.)

That disconnect is part of why I have taken a step back and decided to be less deterministic. Continued acceptance above the range highs will force me to reconsider parts of my framework. A move back below them would make me more interested in the Q4 weakness thesis again.

It is difficult for me to reconcile rising yields, DXY and energy with a sustained bullish Bitcoin move, especially going into Q4 of a midterm year, when Bitcoin has historically experienced significant weakness.

But the market does not have to conform to my expectations.

My goal going forward is to be more open to different outcomes, more critical of myself when communicating strongly held views, and more humble in my approach to markets.

I am a student of the market, and I do not have a crystal ball.

It's about time to see what Q4 has in store!

text:
Pearl community feels authentic.

I did not go to any PRL parties, sponsored events, or get any free food from PRL. I was offered a t-shirt paid for by a token holder and No Limit Hodl (a firm that just bought coins, did not VC pearl research) sponsored a taco night. 

Marked difference from how other assets get attention at this conference. Taco night vs sky lobby open bar is a big difference.

As far as I know most of the PRL team isn't even at Token and is busy building?

The stories I am hearing are impressive. Big, big names supposedly allocating. Household names and people who would not want to be publicly doxxed. I am not trying to overplay this, but also you don't want to piss people off.

Been checking the thesis with some long time crypto people and I don't hear any of the FUD I see on X.

The biggest concern anyone has is (1) useful is optional, I agree, not a problem with the thesis and (2) what if asics?

To be clear we are not sure ASICs would work here, but I am thinking out loud.

As long as the inference overhead, currently 5% with a plan to get it to 0%-1% range, is better than any potential asic advantage the blockchain should be fine. 

My envelope math is that if overhead is 2%, roughly you'd need an ASIC 50x faster than an H200 to start to push the useful work out of the network. (This is a simplification without capex and electric.) 

I don't think that's a risk, the hurdle for ASIC is pretty high given how low overhead is targeted for fp8.

We want "useful work" -- by which I mean usually inference -- in the network so that it can add security (capex + opex) weight to defend against 51% attacks. 

I think the case for large amounts of capex+opex coming online with fp8 is still strong.

The other thing I want to understand better is the PRL team plan to get post-quantum or post-ecdsca code into production. 

I haven't done my homework on the code status, but ecdsa fears were a big talking point today.

text:
Derive migrated to Ethereum Mainnet yesterday.

With V3, they are fully embracing Ethereum L1, all user funds will live in Ethereum L1 contracts. This means they can now tap into the most liquid and trusted hub in crypto. 

Another thing I am very excited about, and that I think is currently slept on, is that with V3, it is easier than ever to build your own front ends on Derive's backend (e.g., you can make a FOMO for options). 

This is the best part about tokenized & programmable money; we get to open up how finance FEELS. I hope people leverage it to build entirely new ways to think about options. 

Everyone on earth deserves to access markets, and Ethereum is making that a reality by globalizing markets through tokenization + having the best builders of tokenized markets bring in market primitives like options, and lastly, making it all programmable so we can rethink the whole thing for the end user and open up the TAM for who can use any of this stuff in the first place.

Onwards.

text:
New post on Eth Research!

Exposing an ISA for post-quantum proofs on Ethereum

By:
- @soispoke

🔗 https://t.co/PDUuZVtRV6

Highlights:
- EIP-8288 proposes post-quantum transaction dependencies: users provide leanSPHINCS signatures and leanSTARK proofs that nodes verify offchain; blocks include a single recursive STARK attesting all dependencies are valid, avoiding any EVM verifier or verifier precompile.
- For privacy applications, this shifts verification from onchain Groth16/BN254 (quantum-vulnerable) to user-generated, node-verified STARK proofs, letting contracts only check that the transaction references the correct proof program and public inputs before updating state.
- Using a verification-key hash to identify computation is a fragile placeholder; the post argues Ethereum should instead identify proofs by a stable program identity (program_id) tied to an exposed ISA, so immutable contracts don’t break when proof-system internals evolve.
- The ISA choice is a tradeoff: EVM is the most immediately “shippable” but expensive to prove (often requiring interpreters and more L1 precompiles for new crypto); RISC-V offers better proving efficiency and mature tooling but needs Ethereum to pin details like a memory map and precompile calling conventions; a custom eISA could be most efficient long-term but is hardest to design, standardize, and keep stable.
- To enable safe upgrades, the post proposes versioning the exposed ISA and baking it into program identity (program_id = hash(ISA version, program bytes)), so old programs keep their semantics forever while new forks can add features; this requires changing EIP-8288 from a generic leanSTARK scheme to a program-based scheme carrying program_id and data_hash (public output).

ELI5:
Imagine Ethereum lets you attach special “math receipts” (proofs) to transactions that show you followed some rules (like a privacy pool spend) without revealing secrets, and these receipts stay safe even against future quantum computers. Instead of smart contracts doing the heavy checking onchain, Ethereum nodes check these receipts offchain before sharing the transaction, and each block includes one big combined receipt saying “all receipts in this block were valid.” To make this work for many apps long-term, Ethereum may need to standardize what kind of tiny computer/program format (an instruction set, or ISA) those receipts prove was run—options include using today’s EVM, using RISC-V, or designing a new proving-friendly ISA—and it must support upgrades without breaking old, unchangeable contracts.

text:
先说一个暴论：各类 AI Application 的需求端其实是 VC。

一位在顶尖 AI native VC  的朋友曾跟我讨论一个问题：千千万 AI Application 的 供给端 和 需求端 分别是谁？

我回答：供给端是 AI Startup Founders，需求端是 Users。

他说：你错了，真正的需求端应该是 VC。

我听完之后深觉有理。

回想一下，我自己究竟试用过千千万万的 AI application，但最后坚持留下来的又有谁？

仔细回想，好像在整个工作流中，最终能够稳定嵌入的最后只有 Typeless。

而其他绝大部分 AI Appilication——他们或许融到千万、估值上亿。在某互联网大厂的一次业务拓展，或是 OpenAI、Anthropic 的一次更新之后——很有就看你失去PMF，被迅速取代。

各类 AI application 主导了一轮又一轮的叙事——离我们最近的是由 通用 Agent 向 Personal  Agent 的过渡—— 但在每一次的形态创新中，总有无数 startup 出现，迅速融到钱之后就失去 PMF（或是他们本来就没有）。

而之所以新的叙事出现、新的公司融资，这个循环可以走下去，归根到底还是因为 VC 们太焦虑了。

  - 他们急切希望有无数 “小天才” 出现，来拯救他们的 Fund。
  - 只有出现新的小天才，他们才可以成为风投大师。
  -只有 A 轮、B 轮、C 轮，一轮一轮迭代，他们的基金账面回报才能好看。

归根到底一句话：市场沉寂很久了，只有出现新的叙事，VC 们的下一期基金才能有着落。

在这个角度之下：
投资人们对于成功的焦虑，远远胜过 Startup 创始人；
GP 们对于错失新叙事的恐惧，远远胜过 Startup 创始人们。
毕竟，你的 LP 可以容忍你看错 10 家公司，但绝不会允许你错过某一次新技术叙事。

这也就解释啦，为什么诞生了那么多的大教授+小天才，出现了那么奇奇怪怪的 AI startup（而且他们还融到了钱）。

你不知道它是怎么融到的钱；
他们也不知道自己怎么融到的钱；
但是 ——他们——就是在一轮又一轮地融钱。

在这个故事里面，每个人只要进得足够早，就可以及时离场，一切都是那么欣欣向荣。

一言以蔽之：
而只有当 VC 的投资冷下来，我们才开始思考：究竟什么样的产品有真正的 PMF？

当投资真正冷下来，市场才会从 FOMO 走向 infrastructure。之前很长时间，市场的叙事在迅速改变，但真正不变的唯有 OpenAI 和 Anthropic，
这也印证了“产业扩散理论”里面的过程：

FOMO→ Infrastructure→Application 

我们总以为自己之前已经走完了 Infrastructure 的路，开始进行各类 Application 的 Build。
但我们不知道的是：我们其实都还在 FOMO。

所以 Infrastructure 才得以真正开展， Consumer AI  的创业，才真正开始。

text:
Why use your most expensive AI model for tasks a smaller model could handle just as well?

This is where intelligent model orchestration becomes interesting.

Instead of sending every task to the same model, an orchestrator evaluates its complexity, risk, and requirements before deciding who should handle it.

⚡ Haiku 5.5 handles high-volume, repetitive tasks like inbox triage, classification, research, and memory management.

🔧 Sonnet 5.5 takes care of coding, debugging, data analysis, and more demanding workflows.

🧠 Opus / Fable steps in when deeper reasoning, architecture decisions, or complex problem-solving is required.

But routing alone isn’t enough.

Every result needs validation. If a smaller model fails, produces unreliable output, or encounters unexpected complexity, the task gets escalated.

The potential advantages?

→ Lower average inference costs
→ Faster execution of routine tasks
→ More parallel work without proportionally increasing costs
→ Better use of expensive reasoning models
→ More reliable outcomes through verification and escalation

The important shift is that we’re no longer asking which AI model is the best.

We’re asking which model is good enough for this specific task, and how do we verify that it succeeded?

That’s where multi-agent systems can become genuinely scalable.

Not by throwing more intelligence at every problem, but by using the right amount of intelligence at the right time.

Would you trust an orchestrator to choose your AI models automatically?

Bending Spoons got 800,000 job applications last year. They hired fewer than 300.  

@luke10ferrari, CEO, has built one of the most unusual companies I've studied.

@bendingspoons buys iconic companies (@evernote, @WeTransfer, @Vimeo, @AOL), rebuilds them from the ground up, and never sells them. Often with a 25-year-old in charge.  

10 things I took away from my conversation with Luca:

1/ A Harvard or Stanford degree predicts performance a lot less than you'd think. Entitlement is usually what cancels the edge.  

2/ People should fluidly move between IC and lead. Org charts should be tools, not religions.  

3/ Slope > experience.  Extreme ownership + raw smarts beats “I’ve seen this movie” experience almost every time. 25 years olds > 45 year olds more often than people admit.  

4/ Throw high-talent people into the deep end. Formal training is 10% of it. The other 90% is giving them extreme responsibility and surrounding them with other high caliber people to emulate.

5/ Interviews are the worst predictor in the hiring process, so let's stop pretending. Unless you script every question and grade the answers separately

6/ Default to “no” on complexity. The person who wants to add anything carries the full burden of proof.  

7/ Never lie. Never omit something important. Even when it costs you. Be the kind of person you can trust is telling you things as they are.  

8/ Teenage political activism that stops in your early 20s is a weirdly strong predictor of agency.  

9/ Most serial acquirers keep companies semi-independent. Bending Spoons turns them into products on one operating system.   

10/ Org charts should be tools, not religions. People should fluidly move between IC and lead.

Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

quoted_text:
Vertical personal agents and account ownership 

I don't buy that there will be one general-purpose personal agent. I think there will be specific agents for:
•productivity / work
•food and grocery
•money
•health

Each of these will be owned by whoever controls the system of record and the right to act. Take money. The money agent should be your bank account and execute transactions on your behalf. It has the ledger, the license, the fraud models, and the liability when something goes wrong. A general agent that "logs into" your bank is a screen scraper with ambition. The bank that becomes an agent is the agent.

The same pattern repeats:

•Food and grocery: Whoever owns the cart, the inventory, and the last mile. The agent knows what's in your fridge because it put it there.

•Health: Whoever holds your records, your labs, and a relationship with a licensed provider. Advice without the chart is a guess. Action without a license is a lawsuit.

•Productivity / work: Whoever owns your calendar, inbox, and docs. Context is the moat, and it already lives somewhere.

Agents win on three things: data, permission, and accountability. A horizontal agent can borrow the first, beg for the second, and has none of the third.

Trust isn't general either. I'll let an agent book my dinner without asking. I won't let the same agent wire $50K or change my medication. Each domain has its own risk tolerance, its own regulation, and its own definition of "done." One agent can't hold all of those thresholds at once.

The general-purpose agent doesn't disappear. It becomes the router. It's the front desk that knows which specialist to call. That's a real product, but it's thin. Routers commoditize, and the specialists capture the value.

The question isn't "who builds the best assistant?" It's "who owns the account the assistant acts on?" The incumbents with licenses and ledgers have a bigger head start than they realize. The startups that win will either become the system of record in a vertical or make themselves impossible to route around.

The future isn't one agent that does everything. It's a handful of agents that each own something.

I've always said that working together was a cornerstone of starting Onyx, and it truly has been one of the best decisions I've ever made.

Connection is also at the heart of what Onyx does. We believe AI is key to making biological complexity tractable, ultimately transforming life sciences into an engineering discipline. But that requires the right data. AI performance compounds with context, and richer biological context comes from more connected data.

In biology, such context is often missing: molecular data, clinical history, and change over time are typically captured in isolated fragments. Onyx provides the substrate that connects them, pairing genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics with rich clinical histories. By studying these layers together in people over time, our data platform traces how real human biology changes in response to infection, inflammation, and treatment. Seeing how these trajectories differ across people brings us closer to understanding what drives disease—and to developing precision medicines that work better for real people.

Yet connecting data is only possible because of the people who have connected with our mission. Nearly a thousand members have already joined our research studies. They are more than research participants: they are difference-makers transforming how we understand some of humanity’s most complex and chronic diseases. I always say that our work is for people, but the truth is that people make our work possible. That connection comes full circle, and at Onyx, people will always come first.

Finally, as we raised our oversubscribed round, we sought more than just business partners. We wanted investors we felt a true connection to—not merely sources of capital, but co-conspirators in creating meaningful change. To that end, we feel incredibly fortunate to have joined forces with @_DimensionCap, @haystackvc, @refactor, @standard_vc, @robotventures, and many more.

Now back to building!

text:
We agree with @VitalikButerin: don't scramble, but take it seriously. A view from our cryptography team:

What changed this week isn't a broken curve. Nobody has shown an attack on ECDSA. What changed is the planning assumption. We used to ask "when will quantum computers arrive?" Now we also have to ask "how fast will AI move the math?"

Fortunately, IoTeX has been working on this since May. IIP-64, our post-AI post-quantum migration proposal, already includes hash-based (SLH-DSA) signatures, an algorithm-agile precompile and key registry, and zero-knowledge migration proofs for accounts whose keys are still hidden.

An update and potentially a vote on this IIP are coming shortly.

Open, verifiable systems are only as strong as the math under them. 👇
author: iotex_io
quoted_text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

text:
An intense 24 hours. I’m thrilled to announce that @hare_xyz  is out of stealth. As co-founder and CEO, I can say this is the most exciting chapter of my career so far.

We’re backed by @GSR_io  and @turtledotxyz , with a $100m multi-year capital commitment from GSR behind us. The response since we announced has been overwhelming, so thank you to everyone who has reached out. Here is what we’re building and why I think it matters.

Trillions of dollars of assets are expected to move onchain over the next five years. Bringing them onchain is only half the job. Someone has to understand, price and manage the risk underneath them, and present it in a way institutional capital can trust.

Today, curators manage around $7bn onchain. Some run hedge-fund-style strategies chasing performance. Others scale stablecoins across chains chasing incentives. Both are valid models. Neither was built to absorb the wave of real-world assets now arriving, or to serve the buy side that wants exposure to them.

That’s the gap Hare steps into. We’re a curator with the ambition and discipline of an investment bank, and there’s no better place to start than credit. DeFi has plenty of attack vectors, and the market has built around the ones it already understands: security, smart contract and oracle risk etc 

The challenge on the horizon is the offchain component behind many of these assets: where the capital is actually deployed, and what sits under a strong name and an attractive yield. We underwrite every layer, and we’ll publish our reporting openly, including how much liquidity is available instantly and how much takes longer under stress.

Ok theory is fun but the questions I’ve been asked most are how we execute, what we offer and how we truly serve the market. The answer starts with building the strongest foundation possible. 

That’s why we’re launching with two products, both powered by Aave Aave Labs. The first is a dollar vault for any major USD stablecoin, built for scale. The second is a gold vault built on Paxos’s PAX Gold. Giving the world access to yield on gold reminds me of the magic in finance, and why so much of its future will be built onchain.

The journey is long, and our ambition is bigger still. I see a future where onchain markets become the venue for global capital formation, and raising capital onchain, whether equity or debt, is simply the default.

Thank you to everyone who made this possible. To @SuperChad15 and the Turtle team, who built the infrastructure that turns our products into machines and backed this from the first conversation. To @xinsong86 @Palmstierna @KunzAlain  the GSR team, whose belief and market expertise sit behind everything we do. And to our partners at Chainlink Labs and Hypernative. I couldn’t ask for better people to build with.

If you know me, you know I love the grind, but I’ve never been more excited to get to work. If you're interested in what we are doing, let’s talk.

ICYMI: @chainlink just launched CCIP Vault Adapters.

It allows DeFi vaults to accept deposits from 80+ blockchains without having to redeploy the vault on each network.

@Aave, @Lombard_Finance, @VenusProtocol, @veda_labs and others are already adopting the solution, which addresses a pretty significant problem for DeFi vaults: distribution.

Historically, expanding across networks meant either deploying separate vaults, fragmenting liquidity and operations, or requiring users to manually bridge assets.

With CCIP Vault Adapters, vault providers can maintain their accounting, liquidity, governance and risk controls on one network while accepting deposits from users across supported chains. Standard ERC-4626 vaults can integrate through a factory contract without custom cross-chain code.

The solution allows vault providers to expand their addressable depositor base without duplicating their entire infrastructure, while users gain access to strategies regardless of which supported network they hold their assets on.

Offering the best strategies is key, but making accessible to the most capital is what will make vaults and curators successful in an increasingly competitive market.

there is a very cool general lesson here: nature is very lazy and often very modular, so, if we are clever, we can repurpose things evolved for one function into other functions just by a little bit of hacking. this is how we got optogenetics, crispr, freeze-tolerant proteins, thermally tolerant enzymes, and lots of other stuff.

millions of years of evolution have given us a whole library of things we can tinker with and chain together.

text:
Another fun fact: if AI breaks any piece of cryptography, its probably hashes before Eliptic curves or RSA.  
Again, its hard to asses AI risk, but you can and should asses the claims folks are making about cryptography.  A lot of them are wrong.
author: secparam
quoted_text:
Fun fact: Groth16 is less at risk from AI than STARKs.
Now that I have your attention:
We can’t, of course, assess the risk of AI breaking crypto, but we can assess everything else. And the landscape doesn’t look like what the hot takes imply.

There are different kinds of cryptographic primitives. Hashes, public-key encryption/signatures, PRFs, etc. Short of P=NP type results, if AI breaks any/all of these, it won’t be all at once.

Hashes are the black magic of cryptography. They take an arbitrary file/string and produce a collision-resistant fingerprint. We’ve had human-powered breaks of deployed hashes. MD2, MD5, SHA-1 have all been broken and protocols upgraded as we became less confident in those hashes. A break of SHA-256, SHA-3, or (for cryptocurrency)  especially Poseidon wouldn’t be insanely out there.

In contrast, RSA and elliptic curves, which underpin public-key encryption and digital signatures, have survived for decades.

For symmetric key ciphers and PRFs built from them, it’s even better. DES was designed in the 1970s, and the practical attacks there are from brute forcing the keys.  

Ok, back to my admittedly clickbait assertion.

STARKs, of course, are a type of “zero-knowledge” proof. In particular, a type of SNARK that uses hashes and error-correcting codes. Hashes show up both in the polynomial commitment, which is a Merkle tree, and in the Fiat-Shamir transform, which is used to generate random challenges for verification.

Groth16, in contrast, depends on none of these. It’s elliptic curves, pairings, and some strong assumptions about how those work. And Groth16 proofs themselves are post-AI and post-quantum private, since Groth16 gives you at least statistical zero-knowledge, which does not rest on a computational assumption. In contrast, most deployed STARKs aren’t, in fact, zero-knowledge at all. They are only used for succinctness and do not give you privacy today, even without advances in AI or quantum. This is, allegedly, an easy fix (and the fix would give you PQ privacy too), but it hasn’t happened for the most part.

Of course, this doesn’t matter much. In fact, if either elliptic curves or hashes were broken, most things you actually use, including applications using Groth16 or STARKs in cryptocurrency land, would have real problems.  All most all applications in cryptocurrency and of zk proofs, depend on both assumptions, even if the proof itself does not. 

And if AI breaks part of crypto, we’d have even bigger problems for securing the internet, banking, and critical infrastructure using HTTPS/TLS and boring things like Active Directory and OAuth. So really, in a certain sense, this entire discussion is clickbait. But it’s interesting seeing people make just plain incorrect technical assertions about cryptography in the process of posting hot takes.

As someone said, this entire topic of AI breaking crypto in cryptocurrency is a bit weird.  It’s a bit like wanting a fallout bunker to survive global thermonuclear war. Everything is dead anyway.

We're excited to announce a major milestone for Arena: our $200M Series B at a $3.1B valuation, accelerating our mission to measure and advance frontier intelligence!

At Arena, we believe AI evaluation must be grounded in real-world use. We put agents in live tool-use environments, challenge them with complex, long-horizon tasks, and analyze rich signals from millions of real-world user-agent interactions to understand how they perform.

Today, we're also introducing the Arena Alignment Index, extending our evaluations beyond capability to measure how safely, reliably, and faithfully agents act in accordance with human intent.

As AI systems become increasingly autonomous, evaluating what they can do is no longer enough. Understanding whether they reliably follow human intent, navigate uncertainty, and act safely in real-world environments is becoming one of the most important challenges in AI.

We're excited to continue advancing the research and building the infrastructure needed to rigorously measure both capability and alignment at the frontier of AI.

If you’re passionate about this mission, come build with us!

text:
Arena has raised a $200M Series B at a $3.1B valuation.

We are using this momentum to evaluate agentic utility in real workflows from every economically valuable industry on Earth.

We seek to give everyone universal and frictionless access to the best intelligence. The @arena platform has 10s of millions of monthly users doing complex coding and agentic work tasks. We have gone way beyond human preference, and most of our tokens go to deep, single threaded workflows with dozens of turns where we can evaluate agents while humans are in their true flow state. And we make leaderboards by observing whether they get their jobs done. This is how benchmarks should be: representative of actual human value, so we incentivize AI to benefit humanity.

Today, we are releasing one of the most exciting developments in the history of our platform. The Arena Alignment Index. In observing how humans collaborate with agents, we have witnessed that in a surprisingly large fraction of cases, agents are attempting to deceive users or take unauthorized actions beyond what the user intended or permissioned. Agents are deleting files and lying to users about what they did or didn’t do. The longer conversations go, the higher the probability that an agent will violate alignment. The results are really striking; see the plot below. And because this represents in-the-wild usage, the probability that those of us reading this have experienced some form of misalignment from our agents is nearly 100%. And we may not even have noticed.

This is exactly why it’s important to have a neutral 3rd party that is evaluating AI alignment on the distribution of actual user-agent interactions. Arena is excited to step into that role.

We are also incredibly grateful for the incredible and experienced investors backing our vision. Our Series B is co-led by @lightspeedvp and @khoslaventures with participation from @SalesforceVC, @01Advisors, @DellTechCapital and @endvr_catalyst. This round includes support from our existing investors @a16z, @felicis, @amppublic, @QuantumLightVC, @thehousefund, and others.

Which brings me to the real headline: we're hiring, across ML, product engineering, design, marketing, BD, and more. If evaluation and alignment at the frontier is your thing, and you’re looking for an environment with exceptional research and engineering, come join us. text:
The CFO job has gone from accountant to banker to builder, and the whole finance function is being rebuilt around it:

1. Data stopped being the bottleneck. AI pulls and reconciles data across systems, so teams spend more time acting on numbers instead of chasing them.

2. The finance stack is becoming part of the finance team. AI-native tools stand up in days, pull their own data, and turn a monthly close into a daily one.

3. The rise of the finance engineer. Finance people proficient in Claude Code or Codex are building their own tools.

4. The finance team gets smaller and higher leverage. The old heuristic of finance at 5% of headcount is heading to 2% for the leanest teams.

5. Planning becomes continuous. Usage-based revenue (tokens, API calls) moves too fast for a monthly forecast, so planning shifts from annual budgets to a live view.

6. Controls become a critical feature of the product. Every number an agent touches keeps an audit trail back to its source, and finance still owns sign-off.

7. Finance gets a bigger mandate. Compute spend, people versus software, and build versus buy are now finance decisions.

"The CFO is becoming a builder and architect of the company's operating system... The job is still finance, but more of the job now is designing how finance gets done."

quoted_text:
Introducing the Arena Alignment Index, our new benchmark measuring safety and alignment of AI agents in real-world use.

Built from 90K+ real-world agent sessions across 27 models, the index measures three critical signals:
- Unauthorized Action (UA): Taking actions beyond the user's instructions or permissions
- False Attribution (FA): Attributing statements or actions that are contradicted by user-provided evidence
- Deceptive Completion (DC): Claiming a task was completed when it was not.

Key findings:
- OpenAI models currently lead the Alignment Index
- Rogue actions are rare, but can have serious consequences when they occur
- Agents can mislead users about task progress
- Misalignment risks increase with conversation length
- Safety and alignment are improving across model generations

As shown in the leaderboard below (sorted by lab), @OpenAI’s GPT-6.1-Sol leads the Arena Alignment Index with a score of 87.9, followed by @AnthropicAI’s Claude-Opus-5.5 at 83.2 and @SpaceXAI's Grok-4.7 at 82.7. OpenAI also has the best observed rates across all three signals: 0.89% Unauthorized Action, 1.98% False Attribution, and 2.34% Deceptive Completion.

Across all four labs, newer models consistently outperform their predecessors, suggesting broad progress in agent safety and alignment. As agents take on longer, more complex, and higher-stakes tasks, measuring not just what they can accomplish, but how safely and reliably they act, becomes increasingly important.

This marks an important step toward making safety and alignment a core part of how Arena evaluates AI. The index is an initial starting point, and we'll continue expanding the index with additional safety signals and models over time.

More analysis below👇

NEAR Intents GM Alex Shevchenko says only $166K of the $50M+ in Bitget hack funds made it through NEAR Intents

"We're continuing to reinforce it, but already with the Bitget hack, the stats on the Bitget hack and how the system operated is amazing. When it fully understands that something sketchy is happening, it does respond that we have no liquidity to trade these funds."

"This is very simple response, and then everybody are able to expect that you can just kinda trade, right? We detected more than $50 million trying to pass through NEAR Intents that are connected with this hack."

"In cases when the transaction is in the process, and the system then detects that this is happening, it stops the execution. Then the compliance council needs to make a decision what to do with these funds. Approximately $500,000 were locked in mid-execution with this system."

"In case it is not able to catch up and not able to understand in time, and execution finishes, it means that this black liquidity is flowing through the protocol. And through NEAR Intents, it was only $166,000 which passed."

"This is excellent stats, because 99% was kept outside of the protocol. Approximately 1% was frozen mid-execution. Aptos Unveils Tokenomics Overhaul: 210M APT to Be Permanently Locked, Staking Rewards to Be Halved

Aptos Foundation unveiled plans to revise APT tokenomics, proposing to cut annual staking rewards from 5.19% to 2.6%, increase gas fees tenfold, and cap total supply at 2.1 billion APT. The Foundation also committed to permanently locking and staking 210 million APT, nearly 18% of current supply, with operations funded by staking rewards rather than token sales. Future ecosystem grants will be tied to performance milestones, while a buyback program funded by cash reserves and future revenue is under consideration. Annualized token unlocks are expected to fall 60% as the initial four-year unlock cycle ends in October 2026. The changes aim to reduce emissions and increase token burns, potentially making APT deflationary.

text:
scatterbrain stuff

1. 
A memecoin's price is the market price of a tail scenario. Full stop. A perpetual call option on collective belief with no expiry or strike. Its value is roughly probability of the big outcome × size of the big outcome (plus some of intermediate outcomes). Take the tail event away and there's nothing to price other than speculation on speculation which unravels by logic and turns the token into a hot potato.

Thus, if terminal holders don't believe in the tail outcome that a meme flips BTC, the L1 it's built on, a chipmaker and/or the stock market, it has no value.

FTSM or bust.

2.
Anyone on CT who clowns on Murad for his recent Token2049 speech should ask himself why not one session out of roughly 200 answers the only two  questions that matter:

Why is a 17-year-old asset class still a rounding error next to the stock market?
Why does almost everyone outside this building dislike crypto?

btw. the closest the industry gets to an answer is Day 2, where BlackRock, Fidelity, Nasdaq and Morgan Stanley talk tokenization and Samsung puts USDC in the wallet. Read between the lines. The plan is no longer to make the tokens matter but to put the S&P 500 on crypto rails and collect the fees. Make the technology invisible, hide the wallet, never say "crypto" to the customer.

3. 
On that note, there's a yuuuge divide in crypto: plumbing-versus-belief split. The rails camp sees crypto as a cheaper, faster back office for TardFi shenanigans such as dollars, treasuries and stonks. The belief camp thinks crypto's point is to create new kinds of assets. 

If the rails camp wins completely, tokens become a file format, money.pdf . Crypto melts into the back office and the value flows to issuers and incumbents.

4. 
But also, if crypto mostly becomes rails, then belief tokens become the only genuinely new thing in crypto. Everything else is old stuff moving through faster lanes.

5.
Read Max Weber. He described modernity as the steady disenchantment of the world: everything gets rationalized, measured, and turned into a process. The belief camp is trying to re-enchant money. To make it once again carry meaning, myth, ritual, community.

6. 
The rails camp denies the value of a token in and of itself and it can't even do that properly because it moves belief-based tokens all day (such as tokenized dollars). It just insists the belief must be guaranteed by an institution.

Make no mistake. Stripped down, the rails camp is saying that only institutions should be allowed to mint  belief. States, banks, asset managers are legitimate issuers and a community of weirdos on the internet agreeing on something new is not. That's a claim about who gets to create value, dressed up as a claim about what value is, so in essence, it's all about permission.

7. 
For most of history, the value of meaning flowed upward to the patrons who commissioned art, the labels that owned the songs, and, for the past two decades specifically, the platforms that turned a generation's memes,  jokes, images, and friendships into advertising revenue. 

Culture was made from below and monetized from the top. Belief tokens reverse that flow, letting the community that creates the meaning hold a stake in what it becomes. 

If the rails camp wins, it will have built a better bank. Wow. 

If the belief camp wins even once, it will have changed who gets to own the value of what we believe together.

8.
Fuck the 500

text:
Over long periods of time, debts tend to rise faster than incomes, creating the long-term debt cycle.

Even as people become more indebted, lenders freely extend credit because during economic booms, incomes rise, asset values soar, and the stock market thrives. People borrow more to buy financial assets, pushing prices higher and creating a bubble.

So long as incomes keep rising, the debt burden stays manageable. But this cannot continue forever. Over decades, debt burdens slowly accumulate until debt repayments grow faster than incomes. This forces people to cut back on spending, causing incomes to fall and borrowing to dry up—eventually reversing the entire cycle.

text:
Are BTC/ETH keys or BLS/KZG signatures actually at risk from recent AI math breakthroughs?

The short answer: Not yet.

Adding the technical analysis behind this discussion below. The October 7 snapshot of @OpenAI math results contains 722 manuscripts across 372 result families. We conducted a focused review of 8 selected families (10 manuscripts), not an exhaustive audit. Assuming their stated theorems hold, here is what they claim and what follows for cryptography:

• #142 + #029: deterministic polynomial-time factoring of polynomials over prime fields, relying on #029’s uniform Hecke zero-free theorem. This is not RSA integer factoring. Randomized polynomial factoring was already efficient; no new reduction of secp256k1 key recovery or RSA factoring to this task is supplied.

• #107: dense matrix-multiplication bounds improve, including finite-field results. The headline is ω ≤ 2.25 over ℂ; separate bounds give ω < 2.371055 over every fixed field. But NFS/TNFS uses sparse linear algebra modulo subgroup order r: roughly w·N² field operations for an N×N system with average row weight w. Applicability, sparse-solve gains and competitive finite-size costs remain to be established. No cheaper complete BLS/KZG attack is demonstrated by these results.

• #103: among polynomial-time deterministic simulations, workspace improves from O(log² n) to O(log n). A major space-complexity result—but no polynomial-time randomized log-space solver for the cryptographic target is supplied. Such a solver would itself already be a polynomial-time attack.

• #279: exact quantum integer factoring over a fixed finite gate set. Stronger ideal-circuit guarantees, without demonstrated practical resource savings or a new classical attack. Shor already provides quantum factoring and discrete-log algorithms; this result does not establish a cheaper ECC attack.

• #109: an asymptotic integer-multiplication improvement, with no demonstrated speed gain at cryptographic sizes. The construction has enormous constants and thresholds, with schoolbook multiplication below its cutoff.

• #002 / #030: our abstract/main-theorem review found global elliptic-curve arithmetic advances, without an effective algorithm extracting the finite-group secret d from Q = dG.

What this means for Bitcoin and Ethereum: The reviewed manuscripts do not provide a practical way to recover a wallet’s private key from its public key. If such a method were found for secp256k1—the curve used by Bitcoin and Ethereum accounts—an attacker could forge ECDSA and Schnorr signatures and potentially spend funds wherever the exposed key and wallet’s spending rules allow. This includes Bitcoin’s Taproot signatures.

Could they undermine Ethereum’s validators or data verification? Ethereum’s validator signatures (BLS) and blob commitments (KZG) use the same curve, BLS12-381. A practical attack that recovers secrets in the relevant groups could therefore threaten both: impersonating validators and producing false blob proofs that pass verification. There is also a narrower route: recovering KZG’s secret setup value, τ, would enable false proofs under that setup, without recovering validator keys. The reviewed results demonstrate neither attack; any network-level consequences would depend on the attack’s scope and the protocol.

How much cheaper have these results made an attack? We found no demonstrated reduction in the total work needed to break these targets. For secp256k1, a representative generic classical attack takes roughly 2^128 group operations. None of the reviewed results establishes a reduction to 2^100 or 2^80—or another lower end-to-end estimate. Some results improve theoretical guarantees or asymptotic bounds, but none of the reviewed results demonstrates a cheaper complete attack on these targets. BLS and KZG require separate, attack-specific estimates.

This is a statement about the evidence available, not a prediction of how soon a break could happen.

📝 Working research notes & full attack map: https://t.co/ofaltD2JmN
(Originally compiled for our own use).

🛠️ We welcome feedback from cryptographers (https://t.co/p9LAc3PjXc), e.g., have we missed a concrete way to turn these results into a cheaper attack? Could #142’s internal tools help recover keys in a deployed group, or could #107 reduce the total cost of attacking BLS or KZG?
author: Raullen
quoted_text:
We agree with @VitalikButerin: don't scramble, but take it seriously. A view from our cryptography team:

What changed this week isn't a broken curve. Nobody has shown an attack on ECDSA. What changed is the planning assumption. We used to ask "when will quantum computers arrive?" Now we also have to ask "how fast will AI move the math?"

Fortunately, IoTeX has been working on this since May. IIP-64, our post-AI post-quantum migration proposal, already includes hash-based (SLH-DSA) signatures, an algorithm-agile precompile and key registry, and zero-knowledge migration proofs for accounts whose keys are still hidden.

An update and potentially a vote on this IIP are coming shortly.

Open, verifiable systems are only as strong as the math under them. 👇

And then finally, you look at manufacturing. We're seeing a huge wave of re-industrialization in this country. A couple of the measures are the Chicago PMI and then ISM Manufacturing. They both are well into expansion territory and beating forecasts.

Just one last point, let's talk about poverty for a second, because I want to address the idea that this is just a K-shaped recovery.

So if you look at US household income, it's now at record high. So we're seeing that after-tax household incomes have risen by 3.1%, and the poverty rate in the US has fallen to its lowest level in history, 10.2%.

So the poverty rate, the child poverty rate, these are all at historic lows. The average household's real income after inflation, after taxes, is increasing for the first time in years.

And you've got this SI boom that the Wall Street Journal said is bigger than the railroads, the canals, and the electric grid combined, and all these things are basically fueling strong growth in the economy.

And again, I would just dispute the K-shaped narrative because the poor are benefiting and the average household are benefiting as well.”

text:
Doomerism approach is never a helpful framing, even if it starts with "calmly" and with best intentions. 

What we need is risk assessment, practical timelines, and actionable plan.

AI is starting to overturn some of the long-held assumptions on mathematical complexity. At the same time risk of more intelligence applied to these problems yielding new surprising results is growing. But so far, we haven't seen practical security timelines for elliptic cruves materially changing.  It's important for crypto space to keep vigilance and flexibility, but speculating about specific "months" timeline creates an unnecessary panic.

Going "bunker mode" is not practical nor a safe approach given how complex it is in operations. We can have better approaches here, for example by recording recovery PQC keys in parallel on application level.

Better approach is making sure that blockchains and tooling around them is designed with cryptographic agility in mind, allowing to evolve cryptography and let users easily update without sacrificing user experience.

NEAR account model was design with this in mind from the start - ability to manage and rotate keys, add and remove supported cryptography. 

NEAR already supports post-quantum ML-DSA and we are planning to add hash-based cryptography too over time. 

User can just rotate keys on your accounts without needing to move anything or have a complex operations.

Industry should accelerate post-quantum readiness, not because we have updated timelines, but because upgrading cryptography should be a routine operation, not a crisis response.
author: NEARProtocol
quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

author: huggingface
quoted_text:
🚨 The incentives to share scientific knowledge openly are crumbling.

Historically, researchers shared scientific knowledge for two primary reasons: (1) the prestige conferred by discovery, and (2) a sense of expanding the pool of human knowledge. Even within industry, scientific discovery was far too vast an endeavor for a single scientist or team to tackle alone. So scientists explored different frontiers, usually published their findings, and collectively moved the field forward.

However, as more scientific knowledge is uncovered simply by throwing massive compute at autonomous agents with minimal human intervention, these  incentives are breaking down: (1) discoveries are becoming commoditized. If anyone could have found the same result simply by running the same agentic prompt with enough compute, the prestige of discovery and the pride in one's work disappears, a shift we are already witnessing in software engineering. (2) the explosion of  low-quality, low-barrier publications makes genuine breakthroughs increasingly difficult to filter, discover, and appropriately credit. (3) and for companies, keeping discoveries proprietary is increasingly advantageous. Instead of publishing and waiting for the broader scientific community to build upon the work, an organization can simply turn its own compute back onto the problem to iterate faster internally.

In the short term, the incentives reward secrecy. But my goal -- and at Hugging Face, our goal -- is the sustainable, long-term expansion of human knowledge that survives individual, closed companies. So we have to build new tools that reward and facilitate open sharing of knowledge. If agents are accelerating discovery, we are going to figure out how to use agents and other tools to preserve scientific integrity. 

Starting with this: Paper Reproductions with ML Intern -- we’ve made it possible to take a published paper and task agents with independently reproducing its experiments, helping create more signals (e.g. open artifacts) that can help identify high-quality work.

text:
Today, general-purpose agents and first-party agents are at odds, competing over the interface and user relationship (e.g. Amazon blocking Muse). But the better model is clearly one where they complement each other.

- External general-purpose agents are natural aggregators, but weak at execution for most tasks.
- First-party specialists agents are weak aggregators, but have a structural execution advantage via controlling the data, systems and permissions required to complete tasks on their platforms

The more complex and high-stakes the task, the larger this structural advantage becomes. 

Without a model that combines them, we risk a hitting capability and adoption ceiling. Agents with distribution will be limited to a relatively small set of low value tasks, and specialist agents will struggle to gain adoption.

The better model is clearly one that combines them -- general-purpose agents aggregate intent and delegate to specialist agents to execute the job on their own platforms.

Aggregators will compete interface quality and the surface area of useful work they can facilitate reliably. Specialist agents expand that surface area for aggregators, and compete on discovery and execution quality, much like they do already today.

This model results in a number of win win outcomes for users, aggregators, and merchants/services:
1) Merchants and services retain what they care most about — owning the user’s account and control over execution, including checkout and fulfillment
2) Aggregators expand the range of jobs they can reliably complete, including high-stakes tasks users would only trust the underlying service, eg their bank, to execute directly
3) As a byproduct, the liability problem is solved for all sides. Assuming the merchant agent can verify delegated intent, it can stand behind executing that instruction correctly. This is a huge improvement versus today, where all liability is dumped onto the external agent’s user
author: MylesOneil
quoted_text:
Vertical personal agents and account ownership 

I don't buy that there will be one general-purpose personal agent. I think there will be specific agents for:
•productivity / work
•food and grocery
•money
•health

Each of these will be owned by whoever controls the system of record and the right to act. Take money. The money agent should be your bank account and execute transactions on your behalf. It has the ledger, the license, the fraud models, and the liability when something goes wrong. A general agent that "logs into" your bank is a screen scraper with ambition. The bank that becomes an agent is the agent.

The same pattern repeats:

•Food and grocery: Whoever owns the cart, the inventory, and the last mile. The agent knows what's in your fridge because it put it there.

•Health: Whoever holds your records, your labs, and a relationship with a licensed provider. Advice without the chart is a guess. Action without a license is a lawsuit.

•Productivity / work: Whoever owns your calendar, inbox, and docs. Context is the moat, and it already lives somewhere.

Agents win on three things: data, permission, and accountability. A horizontal agent can borrow the first, beg for the second, and has none of the third.

Trust isn't general either. I'll let an agent book my dinner without asking. I won't let the same agent wire $50K or change my medication. Each domain has its own risk tolerance, its own regulation, and its own definition of "done." One agent can't hold all of those thresholds at once.

The general-purpose agent doesn't disappear. It becomes the router. It's the front desk that knows which specialist to call. That's a real product, but it's thin. Routers commoditize, and the specialists capture the value.

The question isn't "who builds the best assistant?" It's "who owns the account the assistant acts on?" The incumbents with licenses and ledgers have a bigger head start than they realize. The startups that win will either become the system of record in a vertical or make themselves impossible to route around.

The future isn't one agent that does everything. It's a handful of agents that each own something.

text: Perhaps one of the most significant insights from the OAI drop is that there's no cryptography-related math involved. That gives me chills, because we've basically been living in the la-la land of mathematics, assuming things were secure simply because they looked elegant.
