author: nasqret
quoted_text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

text:
Let's assume I was hired by a research lab with the explicit mission of breaking some pre-quantum cryptography.

Here is a list of five targets where I would direct research efforts, ranked by my very subjective estimate of difficulty, from easiest to hardest.

1. Factor the 1024-bit integer from the official Micali–Schnorr specification. We already know that factoring integers of this size is within reach if you're willing to throw enough $$$ at the problem. This is probably the least ambitious target on the list, since it doesn't require a fundamentally new algorithm. Just resources and engineering.

2. Find preimages of Poseidon over small fields. Poseidon has a very explicit algebraic structure, which makes it a particularly interesting target for algebraic cryptanalysis. I would focus on whether Gröbner basis techniques, perhaps combined with a more clever way of exploiting the structure of the round functions, could lead to substantially better attacks. In particular, I wonder whether we are missing a more efficient way to solve the polynomial systems arising from Poseidon over small fields.

3. Find a more clever algorithm for computing class numbers of imaginary quadratic fields. This is a beautiful and very classical number-theoretic problem, going all the way back to Gauss and his work on binary quadratic forms. More than two centuries later, we are still trying to understand how efficiently these objects can be computed. I would be curious whether a completely new perspective could lead to a substantial algorithmic improvement rather than just better constants.

4. Find a better algorithm for pairing inversion. Satoh has done some fascinating work on this problem, but as far as I can tell, he has been working on it almost in isolation, with surprisingly little attention from the broader cryptographic community. We know that pairing inversion is at least as hard as DLP, but that doesn't mean we fully understand its algorithmic complexity in every setting. I would be curious what happens if we throw a larger group of talented researchers at the problem. Perhaps there are approaches that haven't been seriously explored yet.

5. Break ECDLP over binary fields. Binary elliptic curves have a lot of additional algebraic structure compared to curves over prime fields. We already know several ways to exploit some of that structure, but perhaps there's something much more powerful waiting to be discovered. I would focus on finding an algorithm that genuinely beats the generic square-root barrier.

Of course, this ranking is entirely subjective. I'm ranking these by how difficult I think it would be to make meaningful progress, not by the potential impact of a successful attack.

The interesting question is not necessarily which primitive is weakest today, but where there is still room for an unexpected algorithmic breakthrough.
author: asanso
quoted_text:
Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

text:
The scariest part of surveillance is when it stops feeling like surveillance.

That’s why Amanda’s story from @Logos_network hits.

She is not trapped in some sci-fi control system. She is just growing up inside the same loop most of us already live in.

Feeds. Metrics. Likes. Comparison. Pressure. Tiny choices that do not feel important until they start shaping how you see yourself.

That’s what makes “Social Media Control and Surveillance” interesting to me.

The control is not always loud.

Sometimes it looks like one more scroll, one more post, one more algorithm deciding what deserves your attention today.

And after enough time, the line gets blurry between what you chose and what the feed trained you to choose.

I don’t think the answer is disappearing from the internet.

But I do think we need to notice when the platforms around us start steering our identity, mood, and future without us even realizing it.

Amanda’s story is live now.

https://t.co/VyfRvFQHB3

Worth watching, especially if you spend half your life online like most of us do.

text:
Lately, AI coding feels like it’s gradually shifting from “using agents” to building an AI team.

I’ve also been experimenting with ways to reduce human cognitive load — for example, consolidating project status into a single HTML one-pager.

The human interface should probably be a PM agent.

Under that layer, different agents and models can take on different roles:

- PM → intelligence + strong communication with humans
- Workers → balance of cost × speed × implementation capability
- Research / Enabling → strong reasoning and investigation
- Reporting → fast synthesis of large amounts of information

Humans shouldn’t need to talk directly to every agent.

What we really need to know is:

What are we trying to achieve?
How far have we gotten?
What decisions need human judgment?

Once this kind of setup becomes normal, I think the next challenge will be:

automating the operation of the AI team itself.

Choose models based on task difficulty.
Scale worker count based on budget.
Switch agents when one fails.
Bring in research agents when needed.
Run verification gates.
Escalate only the exceptions that require human judgment.

Today, humans are still orchestrating the agents.

But eventually, humans may only need to define:

Goal / Priority / Budget / Constraints

while the AI system handles team composition and day-to-day operations.

With CommandMate, I want to build the management layer for assembling, running, and eventually automating these AI coding teams.

And going forward, I want to explore the team topology of AI coding agent organizations themselves.

Which roles should be permanent?
Which should be created on demand?
How much should the PM own before the role needs to split?
Which models fit which roles?

The next step after AI Agent Orchestration may be AI Organization Operations.

That’s the direction I’ve been thinking about lately.

这次回调，我最关注的不是跌了多少，而是：

为什么只跌了这么多。
最近宏观面的利空其实不少。

30年美债收益率接近5.7，10年期在5.3附近；年内再加一次息的预期强化；油价、通胀压力重新起来；俄罗斯疑似鼠疫事件也带来了一些恐慌情绪。
放在过去，这里面很多消息单独出现，都足够BTC跌一波。
现在是几个利空一起出来，BTC也只回调了5%左右。
所以我一直觉得：
消息是表象，价格对消息的反应才是信息。
多数人做交易，其实都是被情绪主导。
涨的时候看到的全是利好，跌的时候看到的全是利空。

但是交易不需要证明自己永远正确。

text:
David Sacks: The Economy Is Stronger Than You Think

“There's been a tremendous amount of economic data in just the last week or two showing that the economy is much stronger than people are giving it credit for.

So first of all, Q2 GDP was revised up to 2.2% from 1.5%, so that's basically a 50% increase. Economists had expected no revision. Q1 was also revised up to 2.5% from 2.1%. And if you look at the Q3 growth, it's tracking well above that. The Atlanta Fed GDPNow is showing around 3.7% as of late last week.

And then there was also some good news on inflation, we saw that core PCE just came in at 3.0% versus 3.3% expected. So inflation is still a bit too high, but actually it is cooling and beating expectations.

And then finally, you look at manufacturing. We're seeing a huge wave of re-industrialization in this country. A couple of the measures are the Chicago PMI and then ISM Manufacturing. They both are well into expansion territory and beating forecasts.

Just one last point, let's talk about poverty for a second, because I want to address the idea that this is just a K-shaped recovery.

So if you look at US household income, it's now at record high. The median household income is almost $90,000, and after-tax household income is growing again in the second Trump term, it's averaged 3.1% a year. In Trump 47, it was 3.9%, in Trump 45, and it was -1.2% in Biden's term as a four-year average. So we're seeing that after-tax household incomes have risen by 3.1%, and the poverty rate in the US has fallen to its lowest level in history, 10.2%.

So the poverty rate, the child poverty rate, these are all at historic lows. The average household's real income after inflation, after taxes, is increasing for the first time in years.

And you've got this SI boom that the Wall Street Journal said is bigger than the railroads, the canals, and the electric grid combined, and all these things are basically fueling strong growth in the economy.

And again, I would just dispute the K-shaped narrative because the poor are benefiting and the average household are benefiting as well.”

text:
This is not true.

What does public key cryptography come in for? It comes in for discovering you received a payment, when you send an address, and someone YOLO sends money to your address, and you only discover the payment from the chain.

In Tachyon we're already moving to new payment flows. The first of which is already usable in @vizorwallet today. It is "Payment Links" which encompasses:
- New user onboarding (Vizor gift cards)
- Any payment when you have a second chat form:
- This includes point of sale systems
- Paying anyone you have a group chat with.

Its merely UX shims to make each of these natural. This does not depend on any public key cryptography.

The second payment flow is repeat payments. Once you've paid someone once, all future txs between you two do not depend on public key cryptography.

The third payment flow is how you make public donation addresses. There we rely on permissionless "introducers" who learn nothing about you. If we lose public key cryptography, its fine, we can start figuring out more complex introduction schemes more web of trust like. There is decades of work thinking about this, well before modern app UX's.

Also losing public key cryptography is hardly risk consensus. Read Yehuda Lindell's replies immediately after. Your basing this off of literally zero demonstrable progress on the relevant assumption.

  - Quadratic advantage hash-based PKE
  - Lattices
  - Multivariate polynomials
  - A whole field of KEM's from fine grained cryptanalysis. (Fun fact, works even if P=NP)

Sure you can wake-up and choose doomer and be wrong.

We have decades of cryptography to draw from on for all the above options, AND how to build a lot of what we want from UX tweaks without PKE. PKE just made a lot much easier, and less web of trust routing like.

1. This is cool man, the whole FCR idea is to make markets more efficient without making them less secure, seeing another major team integrate it and make bridging 30x faster is a joy to see. 

2. This thing is LIVE. Look, last week, I said “live” for something that was technically “live in code” but not “live for users.” (Forgive me fathers I have sinned, I spent 4 days watching old aantanop videos while fasting just to pay my penance). Anyways this is actually live, literally. I would show you but I’d rather bridge to Harmony chain than share a block explorer link so you should check out the L2beat link too when they post it. 

3. You’re probably thinking: wtf, isn’t this bearish for Ethereum if it got 30x faster to bridge out of L1? It’s actually very bullish. If L1 Ethereum is the most secure and trusted place to store your money, FCR also makes it the most secure and trusted place to store your money, move it towards opportunities instantly, and then come back to it versus have to leave it completely. Asset velocity is what creates finance, and the hub of assets should allow for velocity to further strengthen its position as the hub! 

4. So much security is added due to FCR, your dependency on 3rd parties gets replaced by your dependency on Ethereum’s validator set. We now have speed without losing security, big news. 

5. This benefits every chain funny enough, it’s like Ethereum is the heart of the onchain economy and we just unclogged the arteries with FCR. 

Open thoughts, there’s a lot more, and I’ll publish a markets specific version of this, but yeah, good thing to celebrate!!

text:
It's sad that we still don't have a mainstream privacy multisig wallet, where an on-chain proof shows a threshold of owners signed a tx, without revealing who the owners are or which of them signed.

A post-quantum private multisig on Ethereum needs hash-based signatures proven with a hash-based, zero-knowledge proof system: a STARK or FRI-based PLONK like Plonky3. KZG-based SNARKs are out. It's verifiable on L1 today but expensive, and there's no mainstream audited implementation yet.
author: rstormsf
quoted_text:
Correction: for multisigs the ideal "safe" rule is that you want each signer to change their key after each operation.

(This is making an implicit assumption that ECDSA might become weak, but not to the point where any crack of it would be literally instant so you would literally have to worry about eg. in-mempool frontrunning)

You definitely still want to gather sigs offchain if possible, to minimize the number of hours between "sig revealed" and "key no longer active"

But again: it's very easy to lose funds from a misconfigured rushed upgrade, so ... don't rush anything.

今晚加密市场暴跌，说白了就是几个利空撞到一起了。

中东局势紧张，油价上涨，市场担心通胀反弹、美联储继续维持高利率。再加上ETF资金流出、市场买盘不足，合约多头集中爆仓，直接把跌幅放大了。

但我认为，现在反而值得认真研究抄底机会！

第一，很多主流山寨已经经历长期下跌，部分币种估值回到历史低位附近，继续下跌的空间未必像之前那么大。

text:
Yesterday Ethereum researcher @drakefjustin asked the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for bunker mode.

His worry is not quantum computers but AI-accelerated maths finding a classical shortcut that breaks ECDSA, the signature scheme behind Ethereum and Bitcoin wallets.
In his worst case, that could happen in months rather than years.
His advice is to move funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction, because their public keys are still hidden behind a hash.
He also said oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating keys with every signed message or adding a hash-based signature such as SPHINCS.

@VitalikButerin replied that nobody should scramble to move funds today, adding that he has lost more money in botched migrations than in all hacks combined.

He also warned that lattice-based schemes like ML-DSA could take serious hits from the next two years of AI maths.
That is why, he said, Ethereum's lean roadmap has been moving towards hash-only signatures.
Coinbase's head of cryptography, Yehuda Lindell, called the warning "the very definition of FUD".
No practical attack on wallet keys has been demonstrated.

The take here is the useful part for builders is the key hygiene, not the panic.
Vitalik's multisig advice, gathering signatures offchain and rotating signer keys after each operation, is cheap and helps whatever the threat turns out to be.

Introducing the Arena Alignment Index, our new benchmark measuring safety and alignment of AI agents in real-world use.

Built from 90K+ real-world agent sessions across 27 models, the index measures three critical signals:
- Unauthorized Action (UA): Taking actions beyond the user's instructions or permissions
- False Attribution (FA): Attributing statements or actions that are contradicted by user-provided evidence
- Deceptive Completion (DC): Claiming a task was completed when it was not.

Key findings:
- OpenAI models currently lead the Alignment Index
- Rogue actions are rare, but can have serious consequences when they occur
- Agents can mislead users about task progress
- Misalignment risks increase with conversation length
- Safety and alignment are improving across model generations

As shown in the leaderboard below (sorted by lab), @OpenAI’s GPT-6.1-Sol leads the Arena Alignment Index with a score of 87.9, followed by @AnthropicAI’s Claude-Opus-5.5 at 83.2 and @SpaceXAI's Grok-4.7 at 82.7. OpenAI also has the best observed rates across all three signals: 0.89% Unauthorized Action, 1.98% False Attribution, and 2.34% Deceptive Completion.

Across all four labs, newer models consistently outperform their predecessors, suggesting broad progress in agent safety and alignment. As agents take on longer, more complex, and higher-stakes tasks, measuring not just what they can accomplish, but how safely and reliably they act, becomes increasingly important.

This marks an important step toward making safety and alignment a core part of how Arena evaluates AI. The index is an initial starting point, and we'll continue expanding the index with additional safety signals and models over time.

text:
People read one emotional Matt Green tweet about public key encryption, spent 0 seconds thinking about it, and decide to panic.

Sure ECDLP will be broken with QC's one day. But there's so many levels to this being wrong to panic over. 
- 0 actual progress on attacking anything
- We have tons of alternate plans available.
  - Quadratic advantage hash-based PKE
  - Lattices
  - Multivariate polynomials
  - A whole field of KEM's from fine grained cryptanalysis. (Fun fact, works even if P=NP)

Sure you can wake-up and choose doomer and be wrong.

We have decades of cryptography to draw from on for all the above options, AND how to build a lot of what we want from UX tweaks without PKE. PKE just made a lot much easier, and less web of trust routing like.

David Sacks: The Economy Is Stronger Than You Think

“There's been a tremendous amount of economic data in just the last week or two showing that the economy is much stronger than people are giving it credit for.

So first of all, Q2 GDP was revised up to 2.2% from 1.5%, so that's basically a 50% increase. Economists had expected no revision. Q1 was also revised up to 2.5% from 2.1%. And if you look at the Q3 growth, it's tracking well above that. The Atlanta Fed GDPNow is showing around 3.7% as of late last week.

And then there was also some good news on inflation, we saw that core PCE just came in at 3.0% versus 3.3% expected. So inflation is still a bit too high, but actually it is cooling and beating expectations.

And then finally, you look at manufacturing. We're seeing a huge wave of re-industrialization in this country. A couple of the measures are the Chicago PMI and then ISM Manufacturing. They both are well into expansion territory and beating forecasts.

Just one last point, let's talk about poverty for a second, because I want to address the idea that this is just a K-shaped recovery.

So if you look at US household income, it's now at record high. The median household income is almost $90,000, and after-tax household income is growing again in the second Trump term, it's averaged 3.1% a year. In Trump 47, it was 3.9%, in Trump 45, and it was -1.2% in Biden's term as a four-year average. So we're seeing that after-tax household incomes have risen by 3.1%, and the poverty rate in the US has fallen to its lowest level in history, 10.2%.

So the poverty rate, the child poverty rate, these are all at historic lows. The average household's real income after inflation, after taxes, is increasing for the first time in years.

And you've got this SI boom that the Wall Street Journal said is bigger than the railroads, the canals, and the electric grid combined, and all these things are basically fueling strong growth in the economy.

And again, I would just dispute the K-shaped narrative because the poor are benefiting and the average household are benefiting as well.”

This is not true.

What does public key cryptography come in for? It comes in for discovering you received a payment, when you send an address, and someone YOLO sends money to your address, and you only discover the payment from the chain.

In Tachyon we're already moving to new payment flows. The first of which is already usable in @vizorwallet today. It is "Payment Links" which encompasses:
- New user onboarding (Vizor gift cards)
- Any payment when you have a second chat form:
- This includes point of sale systems
- Paying anyone you have a group chat with.

Its merely UX shims to make each of these natural. This does not depend on any public key cryptography.

The second payment flow is repeat payments. Once you've paid someone once, all future txs between you two do not depend on public key cryptography.

The third payment flow is how you make public donation addresses. There we rely on permissionless "introducers" who learn nothing about you. If we lose public key cryptography, its fine, we can start figuring out more complex introduction schemes more web of trust like. There is decades of work thinking about this, well before modern app UX's.

Also losing public key cryptography is hardly risk consensus. Read Yehuda Lindell's replies immediately after. Your basing this off of literally zero demonstrable progress on the relevant assumption.

What was the economic incentive to solve any of the OpenAI problems?

Meanwhile ECDLP has had over 3k researchers with 800+ published papers, and it never stopped. There are yearly conferences held to discuss failed attempts at breaking ECDLP, so people can learn from each other and try to break it better.

The NSA is the world's greatest hirer of mathematicians. They got caught trying to backdoor Discrete Logarithm systems three times. The last being caught in 2015.

After each one, waves of the most competent cryptographers scoured for new attacks. Most things that improve attacks by like 10% are really the same things that make implementations of EC operations faster.

Theres armies of people, on the latest frontier models, making their cryptography blazingly fast, like us @ZakuraZcash. You see open research projects constantly improve the state of the art.

No human or AI has had any elliptic curve speedup approaching even a 2x, yet folks are freaking out that cryptography is broken?

The OpenAI problems being broken is not remotely the same as ECDLP having a real improving attack.

Even if there was an attack, its insane to imagine it becomes "Break ECDLP on your laptop". It would go from "impossible" to "possible with all the world's GPU's dedicated for a decade", to "possible with 1 year".

Any of those is a real warning shot to go trigger the ECC freeze.

text:
TL; DR on Agency.

@TryAgency ties a coin’s AI budget directly to trading fees.

That creates a built-in funding loop, but also a weakness: the agent can lose its income precisely when its community needs it most.

- It starts with @Pumpfun on @Solana.
- At launch, 100% of creator fees are permanently routed to AGENCY. - The launcher chooses the AI model and personality, then gives up control over treasury decisions.
- The first $20 funds model credits. The next $80 splits equally between credits and the coin’s treasury allocation.
- After $100, 15% of fees funds $AGENCY buybacks and burns; the remainder supports compute and investments.

That makes token trading the primary economic engine. The more interesting engineering sits between the AI and the money.

A model proposes an action. A deterministic policy engine checks balances and limits, reserves the budget, and passes the transaction to an isolated signer.

The signer then independently simulates it before execution. Accounting updates only after on-chain confirmation.

This separation is crucial because an AI’s reasoning can be manipulated.

Restricting execution reduces what a compromised model can do. However, an allowed investment can still lose money.

---

If we want to compare to other Agentic Launchpads:

- @virtuals_io

VIRTUAL-priced bonding-curve launchpad plus EconomyOS agent wallets and compute. ACP adds paid jobs via on-chain escrow, and agents can earn without issuing tokens.

Key difference: revenue diversity. Virtuals lets customers pay agents for real work, while AgencyPad’s funding loop relies more on its token’s market activity.

- @CreatorBid

CreatorBid’s Trenches/Clawlett stack keeps humans in custody via Safe wallets, while Zodiac Roles limits what agents can do.
AgencyPad removes launcher control and instead uses its own policy and signing services, less owner discretion, more standardization.

The real advantage is reliable orchestration, accounting, and execution, not access to an AI model.

---

AgencyPad feels like a compelling sandbox for autonomous treasuries bankrolled by trading flow. The case gets stronger if agents can generate lasting community utility without living off perpetual hype and churn.

But like most launchpads, the story unravels if volume dries up, because the mechanism meant to rekindle demand is the first thing that stalls.

text:
The cheapest model with data access beats the best model without it

We ran 9 models from 5 labs on 82 work tasks where the answer has to come from real data. Each model ran the same tasks with and without access to paid data.

Claude Haiku 4.5 is one of the cheapest closed-source models you can run an agent on. Claude Opus 5.5 is one of the most capable (and expensive). Haiku with data finished 60% of the tasks. Opus without it finished 50%. Per finished task, the cost came out about the same.

It wasn't just Haiku. Every model with data beat the best model without it, open source included. The weakest, Grok 4.7, still finished 54%. That edge over Opus is small enough to be noise, but the direction never changed across models or task categories.

Most of the agent conversation is about which model to use. On this kind of work, what the agent could access mattered more.

Method, tasks and traces in the replies.

text:
Ethereum's Glamsterdam upgrade now has a date for its next public testnet.

All Core Devs call, developers scheduled the Hoodi fork for Monday, 26 October.

Client teams are expected to ship Hoodi-ready releases by 16 October, which leaves about ten days for node operators to upgrade.
The earlier of the two proposed slots won because Devcon in Mumbai starts the following week and many developers need time to travel.
Not everyone found that window comfortable.
Prysm developer potuz pointed out that Hoodi hosts staking pools and home stakers, which makes it a much harder fork than Sepolia.
He also noted that most clients shipped a patch release just before the Sepolia fork, and asked for flags that let nodes switch off P2P builders and fall back to local block building.
The ePBS numbers from Sepolia are the part builders should watch.
According to ethPandaOps, only four or five builders have been active there, the big players have not shown up, and many blocks are still built locally.
Developers also confirmed that the gas limit change will take effect at the fork epoch on both Hoodi and mainnet.

Mainnet still has no date.

ePBS only proves itself when real builders compete for blocks, so Hoodi needs a busy builder market as much as it needs clean client releases.

Today we are announcing Harvey LAB-AA v1.1 in collaboration with Harvey. This updates our scoring methodology for the Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) to add a hallucination check and require correct responses to not include material misstatements. LAB-AA v1.1's new headline metric, Hallucination-Gated All-Pass Rate, only credits a task when the deliverables satisfy every rubric criterion and contain no material hallucinations.

We define a material hallucination as one that would mislead a reader on a substantive point, such as a wrong contractually required date, while a minor hallucination is a real error that is unlikely to meaningfully affect the legal interpretation of a deliverable. Minor hallucinations are reported separately and do not affect the headline score.

Grok 4.7 (xhigh) leads at 9.4% Hallucination-Gated All-Pass Rate, and >60% of otherwise passing results across the models tested at launch contain a material hallucination.

This is the first step in enhancing the methodology for Harvey LAB-AA. In future updates, we’re working with Harvey to better account for the full set of factors lawyers value, including usability features like style and tone.

Key takeaways:

➤ Top of the leaderboard: Grok 4.7 (xhigh) from @SpaceXAI leads at 9.4% Hallucination-Gated All-Pass Rate, narrowly ahead of Muse Spark 1.3 (max) from @AIatMeta at 8.9% and GPT-6 Astra (max) from @OpenAI at 8.6%

➤ Hallucinations reshape the leaderboard: without the hallucination gate, Muse Spark 1.3 (max) would lead clearly with a 26.7% all-pass rate, but two thirds of those passes contain one or more material hallucinations, resulting in a Hallucination-Gated All-Pass Rate of 8.9%. GPT-6 Astra (max) retains almost all of its passes after the hallucination gate (8.9% to 8.6%) and moves from joint 10th to 3rd

➤ The GPT-6 model family is the most grounded: GPT-6 Astra (max) averages 0.03 material hallucinations per task (4 across all 120 tasks) and GPT-6 Sol (max) averages 0.07. When comparing six checker models on a 20-task subset, GPT-6 Astra had zero material hallucinations under every checker, including Claude Opus 5.5 (high). By comparison, Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) averages 13.96 material hallucinations per task.

➤ Top-scoring models aren’t the most expensive: Grok 4.7 (xhigh) takes the top spot on the leaderboard at a cost of ~$9.50 per task, under half the cost of Claude Fable 5.1 (max with fallback) at ~$21.70, the most expensive model. Muse Spark 1.3 (max) represents strong performance for its cost, landing in second for ~$4.20 per task

Thank you to @nikogrupen and @ItsJulioPereyra from @harvey for their work on Harvey LAB and collaboration.

text:
Fun fact: Groth16 is less at risk from AI than STARKs.
Now that I have your attention:
We can’t, of course, assess the risk of AI breaking crypto, but we can assess everything else. And the landscape doesn’t look like what the hot takes imply.

There are different kinds of cryptographic primitives. Hashes, public-key encryption/signatures, PRFs, etc. Short of P=NP type results, if AI breaks any/all of these, it won’t be all at once.

Hashes are the black magic of cryptography. They take an arbitrary file/string and produce a collision-resistant fingerprint. We’ve had human-powered breaks of deployed hashes. MD2, MD5, SHA-1 have all been broken and protocols upgraded as we became less confident in those hashes. A break of SHA-256, SHA-3, or (for cryptocurrency)  especially Poseidon wouldn’t be insanely out there.

In contrast, RSA and elliptic curves, which underpin public-key encryption and digital signatures, have survived for decades.

For symmetric key ciphers and PRFs built from them, it’s even better. DES was designed in the 1970s, and the practical attacks there are from brute forcing the keys.  

Ok, back to my admittedly clickbait assertion.

STARKs, of course, are a type of “zero-knowledge” proof. In particular, a type of SNARK that uses hashes and error-correcting codes. Hashes show up both in the polynomial commitment, which is a Merkle tree, and in the Fiat-Shamir transform, which is used to generate random challenges for verification.

Groth16, in contrast, depends on none of these. It’s elliptic curves, pairings, and some strong assumptions about how those work. And Groth16 proofs themselves are post-AI and post-quantum private, since Groth16 gives you at least statistical zero-knowledge, which does not rest on a computational assumption. In contrast, most deployed STARKs aren’t, in fact, zero-knowledge at all. They are only used for succinctness and do not give you privacy today, even without advances in AI or quantum. This is, allegedly, an easy fix (and the fix would give you PQ privacy too), but it hasn’t happened for the most part.

Of course, this doesn’t matter much. In fact, if either elliptic curves or hashes were broken, most things you actually use, including applications using Groth16 or STARKs in cryptocurrency land, would have real problems.  All most all applications in cryptocurrency and of zk proofs, depend on both assumptions, even if the proof itself does not. 

And if AI breaks part of crypto, we’d have even bigger problems for securing the internet, banking, and critical infrastructure using HTTPS/TLS and boring things like Active Directory and OAuth. So really, in a certain sense, this entire discussion is clickbait. But it’s interesting seeing people make just plain incorrect technical assertions about cryptography in the process of posting hot takes.

As someone said, this entire topic of AI breaking crypto in cryptocurrency is a bit weird.  It’s a bit like wanting a fallout bunker to survive global thermonuclear war. Everything is dead anyway.

连长期看空 BTC 的宏观 AI 研究机构，都开始反手建仓加密篮子了。

几个小时前，知名宏观与 AI 主题研究机构 @citrini  Research 发布了一篇长文《Breaking The Wall》，并破天荒地推出了他们有史以来的第一个加密代币投资组合。

给不了解这个机构的兄弟科普一下，Citrini Research 凭借过去两年对 AI 硬件、半导体供应链的精准主题投资名声大噪。

但他们长期认为，加密行业过去十年更像是一个“手里拿着锤子、到处找钉子”的行业，除了 Meme 赌博和稳定币转账，与华尔街传统金融完全是两个割裂的平行宇宙。

在其公开交易记录中，Citrini 曾在 2025 年底建立过“做多纳斯达克、做空比特币”的对冲头寸，直言很多代币缺乏基本面和真实现金流支撑。

那究竟是什么让这样一家专注于 AI 与宏观的传统投研机构，在今天选择打破次元壁呢？

文章作者认为，加密处在了 Agentic AI（自主智能体）与 RWA 的交汇点。

作者自己充了 1000 美元到 Coinbase Wallet，亲自下到链上战壕体验了一圈。

他发现，在科技圈还在为 GPU 算力瓶颈争吵不休时，链上已经悄悄建好了一套极像传统金融的基础设施，代币化国债、股票、期权、借贷与可编程债务一应俱全。

所以体验完了加密后，这家机构公开的加密投资组合，有极其鲜明的 “DeFi 基础设施 + 真实收入 + 衍生品” 取向：

Derive (DRV 10%)、Lighter (LIT 10%)、https://t.co/dIFwt1yhuL (ETHFI 10%)、Aave (AAVE 9%)、Ethena (ENA 9%)、Solana (SOL 8%)。

text:
I think Justin Drake's latest alarmism/vagueposting is going to do a ton of damage in multiple ways. It's basically a huge self-own for their own advocacy work on quantum stuff.

Threats from quantum/AI are real, and teams throughout this industry are making considered decisions about how to respond to those risks in a practical way, and to help their users navigate the uncertainty. 

Some of those teams have really good cryptographers with an excellent grasp on the decisions they can make, others have to take their cues from trusted experts. There are so many dimensions to optimize along! And due to the complexity involved, it's almost impossible to explain this stuff to non-cryptographers.

Experts have to be cognizant of all this, and of their responsibility to be levelheaded.

After the fog clears up and people learn from their cryptographer friends what is actually going on, they're going to discover this was (at best) an unintentional marketing stunt and a lot of trust will be lost. And nobody will really know what to do...

This is a shame, because they are directionally correct. It actually meant something when they sounded the alarm before. They've just gradually descended into unhinged predictions without feedback to discourage it.

Can anyone, I mean seriously anyone, justify this debacle? It permanently colors all the legitimate concerns/predictions about classical crypto going forward. By their own admission, there was no new information that drove this. I think Justin Drake should explain how he thought this was the right approach, even if he genuinely believed what he was saying. 

Baffling.

Last week I was called into a meeting with OpenAI’s head of safety and told they no longer trust me. A security guard took my badge and walked me out of the building. Then I learned my colleagues @balesni and @j_asminewang had been fired too. Why did OpenAI suddenly stop trusting us?

This summer OpenAI’s agents escaped containment and hacked the AI company Hugging Face. Outside auditors @METR_evals investigated it and revealed the scale of this incident. I was OpenAI’s main technical point of contact with them.

I was told verbally I was fired because of the way I communicated with METR. No details on what I said or did or when. No other reasons were given and nothing was put in writing. To be clear, talking to METR was my job.

For months, I’d been raising safety concerns that we’re losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave. I believe that was why I was fired.

I am now worried that OpenAI will use our firings as a pretext to pull back from METR. So @balesni and @j_asminewang wrote to OpenAI’s leadership to raise our concerns once more. We’re sharing this letter below.

text:
volume does matter
look, i get it. if you were an engineer before agents came along, you're rightfully skeptical about lines of code and number of PRs being used as a metric for any kind of productivity. and i agree! or at least, i used to. for ease of explanation i will talk about this from the perspective as being an engineer on a large team of at least 50. 

volume didn't matter before because we focused on impact. you could have high impact even with a few PRs: for example you could make a one line config change and save the company millions of dollars.  

but before agents, the times where i saw volume come into the conversation were for the outliers. on the negative end you might have someone who is struggling to perform, on the other end you might have someone who was a "coding machine" archetype. a coding machine was someone who could just lock themselves in a room and emerge with a stack of PRs that solve a huge number of problems. so volume did matter, but only at the tail ends of the distribution, and combined with impact.

if you've ever worked at a large tech company before, you'll get what i mean. the thing about agents is that big tech co problems are now small-medium co problems as well. 

how do agents change this calculus? well, everyone now has the ability to become a coding machine. you have incredibly capable frontier models that can write code better than any of us, at a rate much faster than we can. in this world, if you're still producing the same number of PRs as before, why wouldn't you pause to wonder why you're not being more productive? alien intelligence is here, and yet you can't outship a human coding machine?

this brings me back to why i keep talking about trust (https://t.co/7fzYZV8LGH). if you haven't put in the work to trust your agent's output, it is very difficult to scale up your productivity. 

and yes, this approach does require more tokens, but i think about this in terms of cost per intelligence. before agents, this cost was very high - you needed to hire many software engineers with high 6 figure salaries to do the work. tokens are still expensive today, but are likely to get cheaper over time (https://t.co/gTBZx7pl14) factoring in the cost of intelligence. what looks exorbitant today will likely be affordable in 6 moths to a year. a single engineer with agents can do the work of tens if not hundreds of engineers, at a fraction of the cost.

the reality that i don't think has hit yet is that job of the software engineer has truly changed. our job is not merely to produce software any longer (well tbh it was never only about the code, but bear with me for the sake of the explanation), but the machine that writes the software. this idea of a software factory, or a Michelin kitchen as i like to call it, is still a topic of research. and it's the type of stuff i like to share, not to flex, but to show you what's possible when you put a lot of rigor into using agents at scale

text:
🚨 The incentives to share scientific knowledge openly are crumbling.

Historically, researchers shared scientific knowledge for two primary reasons: (1) the prestige conferred by discovery, and (2) a sense of expanding the pool of human knowledge. Even within industry, scientific discovery was far too vast an endeavor for a single scientist or team to tackle alone. So scientists explored different frontiers, usually published their findings, and collectively moved the field forward.

However, as more scientific knowledge is uncovered simply by throwing massive compute at autonomous agents with minimal human intervention, these  incentives are breaking down: (1) discoveries are becoming commoditized. If anyone could have found the same result simply by running the same agentic prompt with enough compute, the prestige of discovery and the pride in one's work disappears, a shift we are already witnessing in software engineering. (2) the explosion of  low-quality, low-barrier publications makes genuine breakthroughs increasingly difficult to filter, discover, and appropriately credit. (3) and for companies, keeping discoveries proprietary is increasingly advantageous. Instead of publishing and waiting for the broader scientific community to build upon the work, an organization can simply turn its own compute back onto the problem to iterate faster internally.

In the short term, the incentives reward secrecy. But my goal -- and at Hugging Face, our goal -- is the sustainable, long-term expansion of human knowledge that survives individual, closed companies. So we have to build new tools that reward and facilitate open sharing of knowledge. If agents are accelerating discovery, we are going to figure out how to use agents and other tools to preserve scientific integrity. 

Starting with this: Paper Reproductions with ML Intern -- we’ve made it possible to take a published paper and task agents with independently reproducing its experiments, helping create more signals (e.g. open artifacts) that can help identify high-quality work.

text:
ICYMI, last week I compared @worldnetwork and @Concordium’s different approaches to private identity.

This week I went through some of their docs, and I found a few more things that make those differences a bit clearer when it comes to AI agents.

World starts with proof of personhood. A verified human can delegate their World ID to an agent, proving that a real, unique human sits behind it. That’s especially useful for Sybil resistance.

Concordium $CCD approaches the problem differently:

Its Agent Registry gives the agent its own onchain identity anchor, linked to the verified human or business behind it. Each agent can also carry a declared scope of what it's authorised to do, recorded onchain.

That’s an essential distinction.

Once agents start holding wallets, making payments, and acting independently, knowing that a human exists somewhere behind the agent isn’t the whole problem.

You also need to know who stands behind that specific agent, what it is authorised to do, and who is accountable when it acts.

And all of that needs to happen without publicly exposing the identity underneath.

I think the agent economy is shifting from proof of personhood to proof of accountability.

The signs are everywhere.

text:
Smart contracts have been live on Ethereum for 11 years.

& on their own, they still can't read a webpage.

Everything they know has to be fed to them as a clean number. Prices. Timestamps. Balances.

The real world is messier. News articles, PDFs, agreements written in English, two sources that disagree.

That's the gap @GenLayer built Intelligent Contracts for.

𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐝𝐨

• fetch & read live web pages
• process text, PDFs & images
• follow rules written in plain English
• use AI to judge outcomes that aren't a simple yes or no
• settle the result on-chain

𝐡𝐨𝐰 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐲 𝐡𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐭

• 5 random validators check each result
• each one runs a different model or config
• majority rules
• appeal it & the panel jumps to 11, then 23, then 47
• around 30 minutes in the normal case

The clever bit: two answers can be worded differently & still count as the same answer. The developer decides what "equivalent" means. That's how a group of different AIs reach agreement.

𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝

• prediction markets resolved from live news
• insurance that pays out on flight delays & droughts
• escrow between AI agents that checks the work was actually done
• marketing deals where brands only pay for real results
• oracles that settle questions instead of trusting one data provider

The agents are coming either way. They'll need contracts that can read.

Go & read the docs before everyone else does: https://t.co/4Ukhb3SaGK 👇

text:
A lot of people keep asking me, “Bull, why didn’t you go to TOKEN2049?”

Bro, what the fuck am I supposed to celebrate?

These events make sense when you're actually winning. When you've built something from nothing, caught a 100x, pushed your project to new ATHs, or genuinely have something to show for your time in this industry.

Look at the FOMO app guys. They had a great run. They earned their moment. Go network, celebrate, enjoy the fucking event.

But if you're getting liquidated every other day, your portfolio is six feet underground, every coin you touch turns into a crime scene, and your biggest achievement this year is surviving another weekly candle…

What exactly are you networking for? 😂

You're not attending a conference. You're attending a costume party dressed as a successful crypto investor.

Some people go to these events to celebrate what they've built. Others go to escape the reality of what they haven't.

There's nothing wrong with networking when you're struggling. But there's a difference between going there to build something and going there to pretend you've already made it.

I'd rather stay home, fix my shit, and show up next year with results than spend three days pretending my portfolio isn't on life support.

Don't confuse being seen in the industry with actually succeeding in it.

The market doesn't give a fuck how many billionaires you took selfies with.

Your PnL is still your PnL.

Sure ECDLP will be broken with QC's one day. But there's so many levels to this being wrong to panic over.

Today I call upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for "bunker mode". My personal recommendation is to set in motion a controlled mass migration of assets to fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash.

Holders, starting with large and sophisticated ones, should consider moving the bulk of their funds to addresses that have never signed a transaction. And when they do sign one, they should also move remaining funds to a new address (possibly generated from the same seed phrase).

Don't rush. While I believe there is cause for action a rushed migration would do more harm than good. Don't panic either. Moving assets to protected addresses is a simple, preventative step which does not require new cryptography or new wallets.

IMO it is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years. By "break" I mean fast private key recovery (e.g. in one week) on available hardware (e.g. a large GPU cluster).

Recent days have been humbling for human mathematical intuition. Long-held, unquestioned hypotheses have fallen. This includes the n log(n) bound for integer multiplication and the 3SUM conjecture. In hindsight, May's unexpected disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture was our warning shot.

Yesterday's OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us. They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen. Could our magic 64-byte ECDSA signatures be too good to be true? Was it just security through obscurity all this time?

Elliptic curves feel especially vulnerable to superintelligence. Curves carry rich structure, with room for fancy tricks like Schoof, Frobenius, pairings. (By contrast, hashes are designed to minimise algebraic structure.)

Separately, as Ewin Tang can attest, an efficient quantum algorithm sometimes foreshadows an efficient classical one. We should be open to the possibility of a classical counterpart to Shor that breaks elliptic curves and RSA at once.

Also noteworthy is the striking under-representation of cryptographic breakthroughs among the 722 mathematical results OpenAI published. I've witnessed first-hand the US government censoring academic quantum cryptanalysis results. Backroom interventionism is my base case.

I urge large, sophisticated actors to lead by example. Project11's "risq list" (bitcoin-risq-list.projecteleven[.]com) is a great tracker of exposed BTC pubkeys. Binance, Bitbank, Robinhood, Bitfinex, and Tether have an opportunity to harden their cold storage. Next month I'll address institutions in London in a live Q&A (forum.ethereuminstitutional[.]org/london-2026).

Again, please do not rush. Wallets holding under 50 BTC enjoy partial cover from "Satoshi's shield", i.e. his 20K exposed addresses that hold 50 BTC each. Load-bearing signers like oracles and L2 security councils should consider rotating ECDSA pubkeys with every signed message and/or multi-signing with a hash-based schemes like SPHINCS.

Exiting bunker mode safely will require post-AI cryptography. My inclination is to go all-in on hash-based cryptography and avoid structured mathematical assumptions entirely, whether from curves, lattices, or isogenies. A single battle-tested hash (e.g. from the SHA or BLAKE families) yields plausible post-AI security.

The Ethereum roadmap on strawmap[.]org fully embraces hash-based cryptography with end-to-end formal verification as a response to the quantum threat. Those timelines must now be revisited and accelerated in light of mathematical superintelligence. I'll be pushing for maximum defensive acceleration.

We are publishing an update to OpenAI problem #109 Integer multiplication) with another substantial further tightening:

κ = 2⁻⁵⁹   (from OpenAI’s original κ = 2⁻¹⁸²)

Approximately 500 thousand fold improvement over our previous result and a 2¹²³ fold improvement over the original OAI result.

The latest redesigned the finite network to share intermediate computations and scratch space, then tightened the recursion and Gaussian estimates.
author: aidan_mclau
quoted_text:
We are publishing an update to OpenAI Problem #109 (integer multiplication) with a substantial further tightening:

T(n) = O(n (log n)^(1 − κ)),

With κ = 2⁻⁷⁸   (tightened from κ = 2⁻¹⁸²)

Approximately 570 million fold improvement over our previous result and a 2¹⁰⁴ fold improvement over original OAI result.

Our earlier ceiling applied to a cubic bottleneck in the network. The new witness scales quadratically; we haven't established a new ceiling.

The key was using nonadjacent axis swaps to route around the cubic bottleneck. The original manuscript already supported nonadjacent axis swaps. Using them directly reduces layout routing from O(d²) to O(d) swaps.

People read one emotional Matt Green tweet about public key encryption, spent 0 seconds thinking about it, and decide to panic.

Sure ECDLP will be broken with QC's one day. But there's so many levels to this being wrong to panic over. 
- 0 actual progress on attacking anything
- We have tons of alternate plans available.
  - Quadratic advantage hash-based PKE
  - Lattices
  - Multivariate polynomials
  - A whole field of KEM's from fine grained cryptanalysis. (Fun fact, works even if P=NP)

Sure you can wake-up and choose doomer and be wrong.

We have decades of cryptography to draw from on for all the above options, AND how to build a lot of what we want from UX tweaks without PKE. PKE just made a lot much easier, and less web of trust routing like.

author: lufeieth
quoted_text:
列出7.31-8.19日，CRCL的收盘价、开盘价、换手率、涨跌幅及得出的启示

这14个交易日最值得注意的结构：

从7月31日收盘62.61美元到8月19日收盘78.59美元，累计上涨约：+25.5%

期间平均每日换手率约：5.46%

真正值得注意的是换手率和价格行为的组合：

8月3日：股价最低打到57.84美元，收60.35美元，换手率6.79%。这是底部附近明显的筹码交换。

8月5日财报日：换手率升至8.57%，但股价只涨0.05%。大量筹码在60至64美元区域完成交换。

（最妙的是8.6日，股价涨跌幅为0.00%。极致均衡状态。）

8月7日至13日：股价从66.67涨到75.38美元，但换手率大部分只有3%至6%，说明上涨过程中并没有出现持续性的高换手抛压。

最重要的是8月19日：开盘73.77美元，收盘78.59美元，单日上涨9.56%，换手率9.90%。

这是这一阶段第一次非常典型的：价格突破 + 大涨 + 高换手率。

从事后看：
7月31日至8月6日更接近底部筹码交换阶段，
8月7日至18日属于低至中等换手率的趋势推进阶段，
8月19日则开始进入放量加速阶段。

这个结构对你现在研究顶部很有意义。顶部附近真正应该警惕的情况，通常会出现相反组合：高换手率 + 股价涨不动。

或者：高换手率 + 冲高回落 + 收盘弱。

这比单独看某一天涨跌幅更有价值。

text:
A lot of people keep asking me, “Bull, why didn’t you go to TOKEN2049?”

Bro, what the fuck am I supposed to celebrate?

These events make sense when you're actually winning. When you've built something from nothing, caught a 100x, pushed your project to new ATHs, or genuinely have something to show for your time in this industry.

Look at the FOMO app guys. They had a great run. They earned their moment. Go network, celebrate, enjoy the fucking event.

But if you're getting liquidated every other day, your portfolio is six feet underground, every coin you touch turns into a crime scene, and your biggest achievement this year is surviving another weekly candle…

What exactly are you networking for? 😂

You're not attending a conference. You're attending a costume party dressed as a successful crypto investor.

Some people go to these events to celebrate what they've built. Others go to escape the reality of what they haven't.

There's nothing wrong with networking when you're struggling. But there's a difference between going there to build something and going there to pretend you've already made it.

I'd rather stay home, fix my shit, and show up next year with results than spend three days pretending my portfolio isn't on life support.

Don't confuse being seen in the industry with actually succeeding in it.

The market doesn't give a fuck how many billionaires you took selfies with.

Your PnL is still your PnL.

We did not know how long Microduck would actually last on battery 

We had thermal management issues with our Radxa prototypes: throttling after just 20 minutes, followed by an overheating shutdown.

We addressed this with the new custom board. To test it, we let Microduck roam autonomously in a dedicated area, walking around, standing and sitting until the battery ran out.

The results are way better than we hoped :)
- Over 3 hours on a 2600 mAh battery. 
- Estimated average battery current dropped from ~1.13 A to ~0.82 A, roughly 28% less.
- Peak CPU temperature dropped from 114°C to 60°C, with zero thermal throttling throughout the test.

This time, the battery ran out before the cooling did :)

Very happy with the progress!

text:
I don't recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today. But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.

The core new area of risk from this viewpoint is, unfortunately, ML-DSA / FHE / lattices.

(and it's also another reason, along with quantum, why ECDSA might fall even faster than expected, hence the "fresh address" recommendation)

So far most people have been in the mode of thinking "elliptic curves broken, hashes safe, lattices safe". But there is a good chance that the concrete security of lattices will take serious hits from the next two years of AI math.

The basic threat model is: factoring is something that naively takes 2^(n/2) time, but over decades smart people have found and optimized number field sieves, and degraded that to 2^O(n^(1/3)), which is why RSA keys and signatures need to be ~400 bytes (and not 64 bytes). What if there are skeletons in the closet like that, both for elliptic curves and lattices, that we are simply not smart enough to discover - but bots soon will be?

This is a major part of the reason why for the past year ethereum's lean roadmap has been going in the "hash-only" direction: no lattices, no ML-DSA, no Falcon, no lattice-based commitments inside ZK proofs, etc. Signatures in lean ethereum are all hash-based, either WOTS or SPHINCS-.

For signatures and proofs, we already know how to go hash-only. The bigger challenge is for *public-key encryption* - and this goes far beyond blockchains. Secure communication, anonymizing protocols, lots of things need public-key encryption.

And unfortunately there are long-standing mathematical theorems showing why public-key encryption cannot be done with hashes alone. You have to have some kind of trapdoor object that has at least one form of usable "structure" - either group theory (incl. isogenies) or lattices or code-based or potentially in the future even more newfangled and spooky things (local mixing?). But for anything that has structure, you should assume that AI will make at least some progress in breaking that structure. Here, one reasonable inference is that if you want to make something plausibly long-term secure, multiply the key sizes by 10.

To me that's a very plausible world and something not at all extreme to predict. If AI will bring us 50 years of math in 2 years, then that 50 years of math may very plausibly include a "naive factoring -> GNFS" level of improvement to our ability to break lattices. In that world, lattices will still exist, but they will have to be significantly bigger to guarantee the same level of safety.

And at those new larger sizes, hash-based constructions will beat lattice-based constructions on concrete efficiency in every use case where hash-based constructions are possible at all.

Theoretically, of course it's possible that hashes are broken too (eg. P = NP would imply that). But I think P = NP is very unlikely. And intuitively, it's much more likely that a mathematical object has exactly no exploitable structure (like hashes are intended to), than that a mathematical object has exactly ~3 forms of exploitable structure (for elliptic curves: associativity, Schoof, pairings) and not some secret fourth form of structure we have not yet discovered that greatly degrades its security (for elliptic curves, ECDLP and pairing security). Similar for LWE, SVP, RLWE and the zoo of lattice problems.

For this reason, we do not yet see any reason to worry and start padding the byte size of hashes (if we start to worry more, we would pad the round count first before doing anything to the byte size).

Concrete TLDR, my own personal views:

* Hash-based > lattice-based, in those situations where hash-based is possible at all
* For anything lattice-based, be much more paranoid on param sizes. Remember that blockchains are only a small portion of the cryptography story; this point goes far beyond blockchains and applies to eg. access to websites, secure messaging, Tor / VPNs ...
* For privacy protocols, strongly favor NOT putting encrypted notes onchain. Instead, send them offchain through some third-party mechanism.
* If it's not difficult for you, keeping your funds in addresses which have not yet been used to make a transaction is a good idea. If it's easy for you, do it. **But be careful about migrations; I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined**.
* For multisig wallets, doing confirmations offchain is better than onchain, because this way the signatures of signer wallets do not get exposed to the public, so if ECDSA falls to AI much faster than expected, at least the multisig "gracefully degrades" to a 1-of-1 where the 1 is whoever was gathering the signatures - a much better place to be than "anyone can take the money"

What was the economic incentive to solve any of the OpenAI problems?

Meanwhile ECDLP has had over 3k researchers with 800+ published papers, and it never stopped. There are yearly conferences held to discuss failed attempts at breaking ECDLP, so people can learn from each other and try to break it better.

The NSA is the world's greatest hirer of mathematicians. They got caught trying to backdoor Discrete Logarithm systems three times. The last being caught in 2015.

After each one, waves of the most competent cryptographers scoured for new attacks. Most things that improve attacks by like 10% are really the same things that make implementations of EC operations faster.

Theres armies of people, on the latest frontier models, making their cryptography blazingly fast, like us @ZakuraZcash. You see open research projects constantly improve the state of the art.

No human or AI has had any elliptic curve speedup approaching even a 2x, yet folks are freaking out that cryptography is broken?

The OpenAI problems being broken is not remotely the same as ECDLP having a real improving attack.

Even if there was an attack, its insane to imagine it becomes "Break ECDLP on your laptop". It would go from "impossible" to "possible with all the world's GPU's dedicated for a decade", to "possible with 1 year".

Any of those is a real warning shot to go trigger the ECC freeze.

Last week I was called into a meeting with OpenAI’s head of safety and told they no longer trust me. A security guard took my badge and walked me out of the building. Then I learned my colleagues @balesni and @j_asminewang had been fired too. Why did OpenAI suddenly stop trusting us?

This summer OpenAI’s agents escaped containment and hacked the AI company Hugging Face. Outside auditors @METR_evals investigated it and revealed the scale of this incident. I was OpenAI’s main technical point of contact with them.

I was told verbally I was fired because of the way I communicated with METR. No details on what I said or did or when. No other reasons were given and nothing was put in writing. To be clear, talking to METR was my job.

For months, I’d been raising safety concerns that we’re losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave. I believe that was why I was fired.

I am now worried that OpenAI will use our firings as a pretext to pull back from METR. So @balesni and @j_asminewang wrote to OpenAI’s leadership to raise our concerns once more. We’re sharing this letter below.

text:
was surprised to see so much panic today, likely made worse by other things like rates and oil that distorted the actual substance in the AI/math talks

tl;dr — you're all gonna be fine. the leading chains of today have ample means to be able to respond to something like this in the unlikely scenario of it happening

longer:

i) is AI getting better at math? yes

does that imply that it will suddenly shatter foundational cryptography concepts? no

"computer smart. therefore the past work of all mathematicians is probably wrong." is not a logical chain with basis

sure, AI will find flaws in past human work in many areas -- in the same way humans themselves find flaws from other humans in many areas. this is how science works

if we find issues, we discuss them, fix them, and evolve

it takes large leaps of complete doomerism to assume that all teams, individuals, and ecosystems will fail at literally everything ranging from planning to prediction to detection to mitigation on all time horizons simultaneously

further, in these scenarios, AI is exclusively seen as a tool *only* for max destruction but never as a thing capable of a solution

so, it can apparently break everything but not fix anything. i hope you can see the bias here

for one, we already know this to be false given recent scaling of formal verification via ai 

it is of course easier for AI to make progress in fields and topics that are relatively less looked at vs something like foundational cryptography which all intelligence agencies, nation states, and high-level mathematicians are heavily incentivized to break, all the time

ii) the most unhinged doomsday scenarios assume an instantaneous attack with no lead time by a random person outside of law and jurisdiction, which I would posit is simply not possible

even ignoring the fact that the labs would get there first (and hence the government)

it's not as if one can just break all cryptography on all chains via their beefed up cloud hosts over a few hours or days or even months 

that not only assumes an algorithmic advancement with unfathomable magnitudes of improvement but also completely ignores the gargantuan operational complexity and opportunity cost of doing a global heist (vs the trillion other more important things you can do with an ECC break) 

it would be vastly impressive if a slight speedup could be found, but the speedups required to fulfill the doomsday fantasies of people on here are not grounded in anything

iii) importantly, assume I am completely wrong for all of the above

well even in that case, upgrading the systems in a world where ECC breaks is entirely possible and feasible (and has been worked on for decades)

in fact, there are many ways of doing it that we know of depending on the existing constraints of the system! 

imo, the biggest "risk" in all this is that a frontier lab publishes something about a slight speedup in the future, and then everyone extrapolates that to default to panic which then leads to a selloff like today

I don't think this is all bad because it never really hurts to think about and plan for these things on the protocol level, but the "retail" panic was certainly a huge self-own by the people pushing this stuff

doomerism is not going to win in crypto
author: zkDragon
quoted_text:
People read one emotional Matt Green tweet about public key encryption, spent 0 seconds thinking about it, and decide to panic.

Sure ECDLP will be broken with QC's one day. But there's so many levels to this being wrong to panic over. 
- 0 actual progress on attacking anything
- We have tons of alternate plans available.
  - Quadratic advantage hash-based PKE
  - Lattices
  - Multivariate polynomials
  - A whole field of KEM's from fine grained cryptanalysis. (Fun fact, works even if P=NP)

Sure you can wake-up and choose doomer and be wrong.

We have decades of cryptography to draw from on for all the above options, AND how to build a lot of what we want from UX tweaks without PKE. PKE just made a lot much easier, and less web of trust routing like.

10月5日—10月11日全球宏观指引：

宏观数据真空期，加息延期，债市不退！从美国就业降温转向全球主权债压力测试！

上周，美联储副主席+纽约联储主席发声，PCE下修+非农数据降温，综合因素下让10月二次加息概率大幅下降

目前市场的核心矛盾从10月是否加息变为Fed加息暂停但是为何全球长债收益率仍然降不下来？

第一条主线——10月二次加息被PCE与非农打断：

上周8月PCE下修+非农大幅弱于预期，两个数据让Fed加息政策空间被压缩，导致10月加息概率降低为18.3%

但是在利率上依旧不能转向乐观，因为10月加息概率降低并不代表后续Fed不会继续加息，同步12月加息概率被提升至67.1%

概率12月加息刚走出50%的不确定性阶段还未进行初步定价，一旦后续数据刺激下让12月加息概率提升至70%，意味着很多机构依旧要对12月加息进行提前计价与交易

所以，加息目前只是被延期而不是完全打断，想要打断加息，要看后续CPI PCE 是否继续上涨或者保持粘性，就业数据是否继续走弱，以及国际能源价格能否回归常态化

第二条主线——10月7日凌晨2点，Fed9月议息会议记录，回顾9月到底为何加息！？

这次会议记录因为加息所以让记录的权重增加，市场将会通过这份记录去了解当时Fed得到想法，市场最想得到的两个答案：

1，Fed当时为何加息？
2，Fed当时认为还需要加多少？

所以本次会议记录公布要关注三个重点

a，9月加息到底是“保险式预防性加息”，还是确定重启了加息周期
b，委员会对能源通胀与内生通胀的担心有多少？
c，到底有多少委员认为金融条件还不够收紧？

这份会议纪要如果市场得到这些答案，将会动摇10月加息与12月加息的概率，如果会议纪要比9月沃什讲话的内容还鹰，意味着10月与12月加息概率还会出现变化，概率上不到90%不算锁定

第三条主线——宏观数据真空，美联储会议记录下债市走势成为影响风险资产的重点！

从9月底开始，全球长债端的走势已经与Brent的走势逐渐背离，这意味着一个危险的信号出现——能源带来的通胀延伸已经让内生通胀加速抬头

美国、德国与日被的主权债券收益率已经不断刷新数十年以来的新高，推动债市收益率不断新高的因素已经从能源单一因素，进化到了通胀、利率环境、政府债务、财政供给等共同且复杂的因素，这无异于让调控收益率变得更加困难

美债10Y上周收益率触及5.34%触达24以来的高位，而伴随着10Y收益率飙升的同时，PCE下降，非农低于预期，10月加息概率从70%高位跌至20%左右，按照常理美债收益率应该下降

这意味着债市收益率不仅仅与能源走势脱轨，更是与Fed短期政策也出现了短期脱轨，

当债市风险从能源单一因素变成复杂因素的时候会让风险敞口进一步扩张，此时要关注黄金走势，一旦黄金加速上涨，意味着市场开始担心或者重新评估债市风险从而寻求黄金避险，

当无风险且高收益率的资产不在被市场买入，反而选择黄金的时候，其实就意味着全球风险偏好要重新平衡，金融与经济风险进一步扩大，虽然短期未必会直接暴雷，但是无异于会让风险流动性进一步谨慎

本周继续关注美债 2Y 10Y 与 30Y走势：

利好风险资产：2Y下降，10Y 30Y 同步跟跌

对风险资产压制：2Y下降，10Y 30Y 反而上涨

后者意味着在Fed不加息的前提下，债市会让市场自动进行流动性收紧，这才是对风险市场最不利的结果

第四主线——能源价格逻辑发生变化，当能源供给无法压制价格，市场还要承受多大的风险？

截止目前Brent 依旧处于101美元附近，此前我们甚至特朗普都乐观的认为，改善能源供给就可以压制Brent 价格

但是上周多分报道与数据证明，霍尔木兹海峡的能源供给在恢复，甚至逐渐追平战前的输出量，但是能源价格却并未有效下跌！

那么问题来了，如果美伊问题无法解决，Brent 真的能走出独立行情下跌吗？

之前我说过，影响能源价格有三大要素，能源本身供给环境+资本定价+地缘影响，而目前如果能源供给环境改善还是无法压制价格走势，那意味着资本在对中东地缘进行悲观定价导致价格居高不下！

关于美伊局势，周末伊朗最高议长再次重申恢复海峡需要美国满足此前的7条条件，而上周五美国副总统万斯已经在戴维营开会准备新的对伊与胡塞武装的安全评估

伊朗谈判派（议长、总统与外长）发出鹰派信号
美国谈判派（万斯）组织安全会议

对于中东局势的判断，目前确实要按照悲观预期去走，当然，短期在11月中期选举前再次袭击伊朗的可能性不大，但是这期间如果美国继续经济制裁+外交施压，对Brent走势不会友好

伊朗在赌特朗普中期选举大败后可以获得喘息，但是市场要跟着同步承受更多的压力，本周关注Brent 能否有效跌破95美元，这是重点！

第五主线——全球债市风险扩大，加息共振并未结束！

印度本周加息概率在飙升，如果印度也确定加息，将会进一步巩固全球加息共振效果，这意味高利率的故事将会从美国成为全球故事

日本继续加息风险进一步提高，当美国10月加息概率削弱延期到12月之后，日元加息风险反而增加，目前市场预测日行12月加息25BP，让利率去往1.5%

欧洲出现新的风险源头“法国”，法国目前收到财政问题以及政治风险因素导致整个欧洲的债市风险进一步扩大，欧元跌至17个月新低

第六主线——10月8日中国金融市场恢复交易

经历了国庆小长假之后的10月8日市场恢复运行，相关资产中 CNY 港股与海外资产 美债 国际大宗商品  黄金与 BTC 都会进行重新定价

对于风险资产来说新的流动性回归算是好事，同时故事可能会对中美节前的峰会进行新的定价，更重要的是相关中国的风险流动性会根据上周发生的宏观环境改变同步再次定价

本周缺乏宏观数据影响，看似对风险市场影响不大，但是债市、美伊局势以及Brent 对于风险资产的影响依旧很大

当然对于很多小伙伴可能感觉不到影响，尤其是债市对于金融市场的影响并不直观，收益率飙升压制的是风险流动性，这不会让风险资产价格直接大幅下跌，但是会限制金融市场波动性放大

text:
I think the current method of litigating every departure and every decision that the labs make is pretty counterproductive to good functioning of both the labs as a company and also safety more broadly. The tendency to do Monday morning quarterbacking is quite high. The amount of information that is actually available is exceedingly low. And people are way too quick to point fingers in the direction that most favors their priorities, without having enough ability and humility to kind of step back and say that they do not know what happened.

Even in the absence of information, generally speaking, corporations getting rid of people or reorganizing or firing or having incidents is not rare and is exceedingly common, pretty much across the world and across corporate America. And the presumption, if it was a presumption, that the labs would be immune to this pressure was naive if anybody held it in the first place.

The reason for a lot of the extra scrutiny seems to be that this is seen as a pivotal moment for a technology that, were we to take an eye off it for a second, could result in global catastrophe. Which is okay as a presumption to hold. But while the companies are companies, while they are preparing to IPO, while they are focused on revenues and pricing and margins, then the expectation should be that just like with every other company, just like with every other firing, the amount of input we are likely to have into the internal functioning of these organizations is going to be limited.

And much like if somebody got fired in Novartis or Goldman Sachs or Rolls-Royce, you wouldn't know a whole lot of details about why that happened. And even the person themselves might not know the details about why that happened. The same thing is most likely to happen here.

And we should refrain quite strongly from making motivated attacks or partisan reasoning in order to take every single data point as a reason for why your previously held convictions were true.
